package) the fisc-gyg9 entries inside it, which the agent is NOT given. One Fable
agent rewrites and commits. Mechanical gates: codehash identical, gofmt, build,
make pre-commit, make lint (revive's exported rule is the floor), go doc -all
diffed. Then ONE ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION PASS by a separate agent told to
refute every assertion and to re-measure rather than re-read. Fixes go back
through the rewriter as their own commit, because hand-paraphrasing is the
measured defect generator.

WHY ADVERSARIAL AND NOT A SECOND READ: fisc-b8z0's peer review found that every
check in that audit which COMPUTED something replicated, and every check which
ASSERTED something about the tree failed at roughly 40% until attacked --
including the ones done by hand and reported as verified. path.go:53 was
condemned on a one-spelling grep in a session whose subject was one-spelling
greps.

DEVIATION FROM THE REVIEW LOOP, stated rather than smuggled. AGENTS.md requires
three /code-review passes minimum and five maximum per lane. This runs one
rewrite plus adversarial-verification-to-clean instead. The loop's stopping
condition -- no WRONG-OUTPUT and no FAIL-OPEN -- is met on pass one by
construction, because no unit changes a token of code and codehash proves it.
The class that remains is FALSE-CLAIM.

ESCALATION. If any unit's verifier confirms MORE THAN ONE false claim per ten
rewritten blocks -- the hand-editing rate this method exists to beat -- stop the
campaign, report, and re-decide the method rather than continuing.

BRANCH. Everything on comment-sweep, nothing squashed. The rewriter's commit and
each fix commit stay separate so that introduced-by-fix attribution is a git log
query rather than archaeology: fisc-pm8f recorded that number as 8 when per
finding it was 27, and only one of the caveats lane's six was labelled as such in
its own commit message.
notes:
================= MEASURED 2026-09-03, ANSWERING THE OWNER'S THREE QUESTIONS ===

Asked: how much narration is there; can a consumer use the exported API without
reading the code; are the comments on tests useful.

1. NARRATION IS 7% OF BLOCKS AND 16% OF COMMENT LINES, in production and in
   tests alike. Narrated blocks run about 2.3x the average block length, which
   is why a per-LINE grep reports 1.1% and badly understates it -- the marker is
   one line of a long paragraph.

     production Go   1,636 blocks / 10,969 lines   108 blocks (7%) = 1,752 lines
     test Go         1,671 blocks /  7,749 lines   124 blocks (7%) = 1,259 lines

   ~3,000 lines across the tree. Commonest markers: "used to" (91), "no longer"
   (42), "before this" (40), "the old X" (31), "until now" (15). FIVE "Found by"
   CREDIT LINES SURVIVE IN PRODUCTION despite fisc-pm8f's lane 1 deleting 66 --
   evidence that the earlier narration pass was incomplete, not that it was
   wrong.

   CAVEAT THAT BOUNDS ANY DELETE. fisc-pm8f already measured that of 62 comments
   matching a self-correction grep, only 14 were the erratum the rule names; the
   rest were design history explaining why the code has its shape, or mutation
   proofs. So the operation is "keep the rule, drop the history that argued for
   it", per block, not a grep-and-delete.

2. THE EXPORTED API IS THE WEAK SPOT, AND IT IS THE ONE THE OWNER CARES MOST
   ABOUT. fisc-b8z0 judged 143 exported symbols from `go doc -all` alone, bodies
   hidden: 60% SUFFICIENT, 24% UNDER-DOCUMENTED, 10% LEAKY, 6% MISSING. A
   QUARTER OF THE SAMPLED PUBLIC API CANNOT BE USED CORRECTLY FROM ITS DOC --
   iostreams.Test returns three identical *bytes.Buffer and never says which is
   which; cmdutil.Hintf's nil passthrough is undocumented while its sibling
   WithHint documents it; amount.Parse never says a rejection is a *ParseError
   nor whether ErrAbsent is bare or wrapped. That sample is 143 of the ~542
   exported identifiers revive requires a doc on, so roughly a quarter of the
   API has been assessed at all.

   This is the only part of the brief that is ADDITIVE, and it is cheap to
   verify: hide the body, hand a consumer the doc, see if they can use it.

3. TEST COMMENTS ARE THE MOST DEFENSIBLE CATEGORY PER LINE, which was not the
   expected answer and had never been measured. 1,671 blocks / 7,749 lines.
   Mutation proofs -- the class AGENTS.md names as unrecoverable -- are only 10%
   of those lines (80 blocks). But a random sample of ten blocks of 3+ lines
   found SEVEN carrying something no reader recovers from the code: the printed
   control total a fixture is checked against, why a fixture is synthetic rather
   than copied from data/extracted/ (no page of that shape exists in the
   corpus), the parentheses-mean-negative document fact, the CSS specificity
   forensics behind a pinned stylesheet rule, and what failure the assertion
   exists to prevent. A test's REASON FOR EXISTING is never in its body.
   The exceptions were restatements of the test's own name, and narration about
   a predecessor test -- which is (1), not a test-comment problem.

WHAT THIS SAYS THE WORK IS, cheapest first:
  A. Narration, ~3,000 lines, production and tests. Deletion with judgement.
     Needs no adversarial pass: a deletion cannot introduce a false claim.
  B. The exported API, additive, ~542 symbols. Highest value in the brief.
  C. Internal/inline, 51% of lines droppable (fisc-b8z0, a floor). Delete-only.
  D. Test comments other than narration: leave them.

WHY NOT THE REWRITE THIS BEAD SPECIFIES. Measured on unit 1 (internal/geom):
42.5 minutes of agent wall-clock and 411k subagent tokens for 148 comment lines,
extrapolating to ~90 hours and ~52M tokens for the tree's 18,718. And it GREW
the file 148 -> 174 lines (+18%), where an earlier unrestricted run of the same
task on the same file cut it 11% -- the five additions to the rules pack
("keep the consequence", "enumerations complete", "grow an under-documented
export") traded volume for correctness. The verification cost is driven entirely
by claims WRITTEN OR KEPT, which is why deletion is roughly a tenth of the price.
close_reason: IT PRODUCED ITS ANSWER AND THE ANSWER IS NO. One pilot unit (internal/geom, 148 comment lines, 2 files) ran the full protocol -- Fable rewrite, adversarial verification, Fable fix pass -- at 42.5 minutes of agent wall-clock and 411k subagent tokens. Extrapolated over the tree's 18,718 in-scope comment lines, and the same answer whether scaled by lines or by the ~9,700 factual claims at the pilot's density: ~90 HOURS AND ~52M TOKENS. AND IT GREW THE FILE: 148 -> 174 comment lines, +18%, where an earlier unrestricted run on the same two files cut 11% -- the five additions to the rules pack traded volume for correctness, so this was never a trimming exercise. THE STRUCTURAL LESSON, which is what makes the successors cheap: verification cost attaches entirely to claims WRITTEN OR KEPT, and a deletion cannot introduce a false claim, so the droppable half needs no adversary and is roughly a tenth of the price. WHAT IT LEFT BEHIND: tools/codehash with its mutation proof, and three commits on the local branch comment-sweep (71fd344, 76fec71, 123eca1), which is abandoned unmerged and cherry-pickable. Findings filed rather than left here: fisc-1u2h, fisc-sn7v, fisc-fbnj, fisc-jway, fisc-ynuo, fisc-jnuf. The verification pass earned its place -- it attacked 77 claims, 68 survived, and of the 3 it refuted one was introduced by the rewrite itself and two were pre-existing defects it walked past.

title: A dirty-tree build stamps a clean commit hash into published provenance
description:
internal/build's Get() reads debug.ReadBuildInfo() settings "vcs.revision" and
"vcs.time" and IGNORES "vcs.modified". So a binary built from a working tree with
uncommitted changes reports the last commit's hash as though it were the source
of the running code.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE MORE THAN IN MOST PROJECTS. That hash is not decoration. It
reaches published output through two fields:
  - check.Report.GeneratedBy, serialized as json:"generated_by" -- "the binary
    that ran the checks, as `fisc --version` prints";
  - export's View/document GeneratedBy, "the tool and version that wrote the
    output".

This project's whole premise is that every published figure traces to a source,
and fisc verify fails when a link in that chain breaks. The chain includes WHICH
BINARY produced the artifact. A dirty build breaks that link silently and
nothing goes red -- the hash is well-formed, it just describes code that was not
what ran.

THE FIX IS THE GO CONVENTION: read the "vcs.modified" setting and mark the commit
when it is "true" (the usual spelling is a "+dirty" or "-dirty" suffix). Note the
ldflags path short-circuits before ReadBuildInfo is consulted at all -- Get()
returns early when both Commit and Date are set from ldflags -- so a release
build is unaffected and this only concerns builds made from a checkout, which is
every build a contributor or CI-without-ldflags makes.

PROVE IT CAN FAIL: build from a tree with an uncommitted edit, run
`./bin/fisc --version`, and compare against `git status --porcelain`. Today the
version line cannot tell the two states apart. A test can assert the marker by
constructing an Info from synthetic debug.BuildSetting values rather than by
dirtying the tree.

FOUND BY the blind-read comment audit (fisc-b8z0), as a byproduct: a reader given
internal/build/build.go with its comments stripped noticed that the switch
handles two vcs keys and not the third. Neither the comments nor any test
mentioned the omission, which is why it survived -- it is an ABSENCE, and absences
are what neither a comment sweep nor a diff review looks for.
notes:
QUALIFICATION, from the leaf-a scoring pass, and it narrows the blast radius.

`make build` injects Version from `git describe --dirty` and -X-stamps Commit and
Date (Makefile). Get() returns early when both Commit and Date are set, so that
path never reaches ReadBuildInfo at all -- and the "--dirty" suffix on Version
means a make-built binary DOES disclose a dirty tree, by accident of the Version
string rather than through anything this package does.

So the exposure is narrower than first filed: it is a plain `go build` or
`go run` from a checkout, and any CI or release path that does not pass ldflags.
That is still the path a contributor uses by default, and internal/build has no
test file at all, so nothing pins either behaviour.

Also confirmed: "vcs.modified" appears nowhere in the repository.
close_reason: internal/build now reads vcs.modified and Info carries Modified, which String renders as a +dirty marker. Proved end-to-end on a genuinely dirty tree: go build (no ldflags) went from 'dev (f6823d83aee4)' to 'dev (f6823d83aee4+dirty)'. Every published generated_by routes through build.Get().String(), so the marker reaches check.Report.GeneratedBy and export's document GeneratedBy without further change. Measured and worth knowing: make build was never the affected path -- the Makefile's VERSION uses git describe --dirty, so it already printed 'f6823d8-dirty'; the gap was builds without ldflags.

title: Measure whether the comments are needed: two blind tests over a 335-block pilot
description:
MEASUREMENT ONLY. The tree does not change; artifacts live in /tmp and the result
lands in this bead's notes.

THE QUESTION. Production Go is 40% comment by line -- 10,938 lines across 1,631
blocks against 15,052 lines of code -- and nobody knows how much of it a reader
could have got from the code itself.

WHAT REFRAMED IT. Splitting the 1,631 production blocks by what they sit on:

  doc on EXPORTED      330 blocks   2,230 lines   avg 6.8
  doc on unexported    492 blocks   4,016 lines   avg 8.2
  inline, in a body    791 blocks   4,413 lines   avg 5.6
  package doc           18 blocks     279 lines   avg 15.5

THE INTERNALS CARRY NEARLY TWICE THE API'S DOC PROSE, IN LONGER BLOCKS. That is
backwards. An exported symbol's comment is a contract that spares a consumer
reading the code; an unexported one sits next to the code and can be terse when
the function is short and unsurprising. Exported docs are 20% of comment lines;
78% is on unexported functions and inside bodies.

SO THERE ARE TWO TESTS, NOT ONE, because the standard is not the same.

  UNEXPORTED AND INLINE -- hide the comment, show the code. Could a reader
  recover it? Target population: 1,283 blocks / 8,429 lines.
    RECOVERED         the blind account says the same thing. Drop or shrink.
    MISSED-REASONING  states something a blind reader could not infer. Keep --
                      and record how few lines would carry it.
    MISSED-EXTRINSIC  cites a PDF page, a dollar figure, a measurement. Nobody
                      recovers these from code; scored separately so they do not
                      swamp the result.
    CONTRADICTED      blind says X, comment says not-X. Either the comment is
                      STALE (a finding, and the prize) or the code misleads.

  EXPORTED -- hide the BODY, show the signature and doc. The blind-read test is
  actively wrong here: recoverable-from-code is not a defect when the point is
  not having to read the code.
    SUFFICIENT        a consumer could use it correctly.
    UNDER-DOCUMENTED  omits what a caller must know -- error conditions, zero and
                      nil behaviour, whether an argument is mutated, ordering,
                      units.
    LEAKY             documents implementation the caller does not need.
    WRONG             contradicts the body. Stale, and a finding.

So the sweep this informs may INCREASE prose on the 330 exported blocks while
cutting the other 1,283.

SCORED PER SENTENCE, NOT PER BLOCK. amount.Parse is the worked example: its
"Accepted: ..." list is contract, while "a leading - is almost always a
dash-as-zero glued on from the previous column" is a document quirk no reader
recovers and a blind reader gets actively WRONG. Same block, opposite verdicts.
Report block-level and line-level rates.

PILOT, 335 blocks over 17 files, chosen so each test gets a real sample:
  leaf rung per go list -deps (pkg/iostreams, pkg/cmdutil, internal/build,
    internal/amount, internal/geom, internal/corpus) -- 11 files, 110 exported,
    132 target. Nearly pure API: the clean sample for the consumer test.
  internal/registry -- 3 files, 32 exported, 79 target. Mixed, real document
    quirks.
  pkg/cmd/export -- 3 files, 7 exported, 87 target. The most internals-heavy
    package small enough to pilot; without it the 78% of prose we most want to
    measure has almost no sample.

Tests are out of scope: 1,666 more blocks, and their mutation proofs need a
different bar again.

WHY DELETE-THEN-RESTORE IS THE RIGHT SWEEP IF THIS SAYS GO. fisc-pm8f's 33
review findings ALL came from paraphrasing -- roughly two new false claims per
ten hand-edited blocks, invisible to every gate. A binary keep-verbatim-or-drop
decision cannot introduce a false claim.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT REACH.
  - Strings are not comments. internal/check's printed reasons carry 204
    hand-typed numbers and are what fisc verify shows a reader. fisc-a8dm.
  - revive's `exported` rule is a floor: 542 exported identifiers require a doc
    comment, so those 330 blocks can shrink but not vanish.
  - make js breaks if site/app.js is stripped -- layout.mjs pins eight phrases
    living in app.js's own comments.

HONESTY CHECKS ON THE MEASUREMENT ITSELF.
  - Every blind claim must cite the lines supporting it, so a confident
    hallucination is catchable. Without that a needed comment scores RECOVERED
    and the measurement inverts.
  - Every CONTRADICTED and WRONG verdict is confirmed by hand before it counts.
  - Calibration: re-run one blind read with a different framing and report the
    disagreement rate whether or not it flatters the method.
  - No extrapolation to internal/check (373 target blocks, 29% of the total)
    without the per-package spread -- its prose is unusually citation-heavy, so
    its keep-rate is likely higher than any pilot package's.
notes:
METHOD LIMITATIONS, recorded during the run rather than after, because each one
bounds how the numbers may be read.

1. ERROR STRINGS SURVIVE STRIPPING, AND THIS PROJECT PUTS ITS LORE IN THEM.
   The single largest confound. 136 long string literals in production Go carry a
   because-clause, a document reference or a worked example. The blind reader
   recovered amount.Parse's whole "Rejected, because..." paragraph purely from the
   refusal messages, which say the same thing in nearly the same words. One
   reader put it better than I did: "the USER's rationale survived stripping; the
   MAINTAINER's did not."
   CONSEQUENCE: a RECOVERED verdict here often means "a second copy of an error
   string", not "obvious from the control flow". That is still a real finding --
   the string is the better home, because a reader meets it at the moment it
   matters -- but it is a different finding from "the code is self-evident", and
   the report must not conflate them.

2. THE STRIP LEAVES BLANK LINES WHERE COMMENTS WERE. go/printer preserves the
   blank separation, so a blind reader can see THAT something was explained
   without seeing WHAT. One reader noticed this explicitly and said the gaps
   corroborated its CANNOT-TELL list.
   DIRECTION OF BIAS: toward MISSED. A visible gap prompts "something was here",
   which inflates the comment-earns-its-place rate and deflates the droppable
   rate. So THE DROPPABLE FIGURES ARE A FLOOR, not a ceiling. Worth fixing in any
   rerun by collapsing the blank runs the strip creates.

3. A BLIND READER PRODUCES CONFIDENT WRONG FINDINGS, WHICH IS WHY EVERY CLAIM IS
   CHECKED. Worked example: the registry read reported "Assignable defaults to
   TRUE at load and FALSE at query" as an inconsistency. Checked -- load.go folds
   an ABSENT yaml field to true; registry.go's Assignable(slug) returns false for
   an UNKNOWN SLUG. Two different questions, no inconsistency, and load.go's own
   comment says the fold exists "so no caller has to". Plausible, specific,
   line-cited, and wrong.
   This is why the line-citation requirement is load-bearing and why no verdict
   is accepted without checking it against the tree.

4. ONE FILE AT A TIME UNDER-REPORTS. Reading a package in isolation means a
   symbol whose purpose is only visible from its CALLERS scores as CANNOT-TELL.
   internal/amount's MaxDecimals and DigitCents both scored that way for exactly
   this reason. Bias is again toward MISSED, so again the droppable rate is a
   floor.
================= RESULTS, 2026-09-02. PARTIAL: see WHAT IS UNFINISHED. =========

THE EXPORTED SIDE IS COMPLETE. All 8 pilot packages, 143 exported symbols, judged
from `go doc -all` alone with the bodies hidden -- can a consumer use this
correctly without reading the code?

  SUFFICIENT          86   60%
  UNDER-DOCUMENTED    34   24%
  LEAKY               15   10%
  MISSING              8    6%   (all Error()/Unwrap() on documented error types)

  by package (symbols / SUFF / UNDER / LEAKY / MISSING)
    pkg/iostreams      6   3  2  1  0        internal/corpus   27  18  6  3  0
    pkg/cmdutil       24  10  8  1  5        internal/registry 40  26  9  3  2
    internal/build     6   4  1  1  0        pkg/cmd/export     7   2  2  3  0
    internal/amount   15  10  2  2  1        internal/geom     18  13  4  1  0

  SO A QUARTER OF THE PUBLIC API CANNOT BE USED CORRECTLY FROM ITS DOC. The five
  worst: iostreams.Test returns three identical *bytes.Buffer and never says
  which is which, so a wrong guess passes silently; cmdutil.Hintf's nil
  passthrough is undocumented while its sibling WithHint documents it, so a nil
  turns success into reported failure; geom.Grid.Band states no bounds contract
  while its sibling Index returns -1 by design (filed, fisc-yjjb); the four
  singular registry lookups are silent about copying while the plural forms
  promise copies, on a type that promises concurrency safety; amount.Parse never
  says a rejection is a *ParseError nor whether ErrAbsent is bare or wrapped.

  THE LEAKY 15 CLUSTER ON ONE SHAPE: unexported identifiers a caller cannot see
  (categoryEntry, decodeFile, assetPath, buildAll), expiring corpus censuses
  (45 ellipses, 208k words, 786 artifacts), and past-tense fix narration
  ("caught by review", "until now no Builder could reach it"). internal/build.Get
  leaks its whole 23-line body into godoc because it is a var over
  sync.OnceValue.

THE UNEXPORTED + INLINE SIDE SPLITS HARD BY DEPTH, which is what the pilot was
shaped to detect and is the single most useful result here:

  internal/amount   (leaf, pure algorithm)   15 blocks  41 lines
                    12 of 15 blocks fully droppable (80%),  76% of lines
  pkg/cmd/export    (composition root)       24 of 87 blocks sampled, 140 lines
                     4 of 24 blocks fully droppable (17%),  49% of lines

  THE REASON IS LEGIBLE AND IT GENERALISES. A leaf algorithm's comments mostly
  restate control flow, and a reader with the code recovers them. A composition
  root's comments are mostly ARCHITECTURAL -- "views lives in the command and not
  in internal/export, and that is what keeps that package's stated property
  true"; "the label registry is loaded here so internal/project stays decoupled";
  "extracted from the loop so a test can hand it a state the real repository is
  never in". None of that is in the code, because it is about the RELATIONSHIP
  BETWEEN packages, and the code in front of you is one side of it.

  SO THE KEEP-RATE TRACKS HOW MUCH OF A COMMENT IS ABOUT SOMETHING OTHER THAN THE
  CODE IT SITS ON. That is a better predictor than exported-vs-unexported, and it
  says internal/check (373 target blocks) will be nearer cmd-export than amount.

THE SINGLE BEST CASE IN THE SAMPLE, worth keeping as the worked example of a
comment earning its place: export.go's two-line "Validate canonicalises it, so
after validation it is absolute and symlink-resolved". The blind reader's own
CANNOT-TELL list asks, in as many words, "What does ResolveOutputDir do (abs?
symlink resolution?)". Two lines, answering the exact question a reader forms.

AND THE WORST: amount.Parse's four-line "Rejected, because..." paragraph, which
the blind reader reproduced almost verbatim -- from the REFUSAL STRINGS, which
say the same thing in nearly the same words. Four declarations away, the
four-word trailing comment // "0" parses normally was called "the single least
self-explanatory line in the file". Length and value are uncorrelated.

WHAT IS UNFINISHED. Four scoring agents died on a session limit mid-run. The
blind-read accounts for leaf-a (iostreams, build, geom), leaf-b (cmdutil,
corpus) and registry are COMPLETE and on disk at /tmp/ca/accounts/*.md, along
with the block inventories at /tmp/ca/blocks-*.json. Scoring those three is
~180 target blocks and needs no new blind reads. cmd-export is sampled 24 of 87,
not scored whole. Note /tmp is not durable -- rerun the strip and blind reads if
it has been cleared.

BYPRODUCT DEFECTS, both verified and filed: fisc-qz2w (P2, a dirty-tree build
stamps a clean commit hash into published provenance) and fisc-yjjb (P3, geom's
dead Page.Width/Height and Band panicking on Index's sentinel). Neither is a
comment defect. Both are ABSENCES, which is what no comment sweep and no diff
review looks for, and both were found by a reader who had nothing but the code.
============ COMPLETE. All four killed scorers rerun, one at a time. ===========

THE ANSWER, over 343 blocks / 1,826 lines across 8 packages.

  UNEXPORTED + INLINE   219 blocks  1,063 lines   51% OF LINES DROPPABLE
    internal/amount      15    41   76%      leaf-b  cmdutil/corpus  27  102  60%
    leaf-a io/build/geom 11    43   63%      pkg/cmd/export          87  553  42%
    internal/registry    79   324   61%

  EXPORTED + PACKAGE DOC 124 blocks  763 lines    6% droppable
    95 SUFFICIENT, 21 UNDER-DOCUMENTED, 4 CONTRADICTED, 3 LEAKY, 1 PARTIAL

So the two standards differ by roughly 8x, and the answer to "are any truly
needed" is: on the API, nearly all of them, and 21 need MORE than they have; in
the internals, about half are recoverable from the code and can go.

THE DEPTH STORY IS REAL BUT NARROWER THAN I FIRST CLAIMED. I predicted a gradient
by depth. What the numbers show is ONE OUTLIER: pkg/cmd/export, the composition
root, at 42%, against a 60-76% cluster for everything else. Its comments are
architectural -- "views lives in the command and not in internal/export, and that
is what keeps that package's stated property true" -- which is about a
RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN packages, and the code in front of you is one side of it.
internal/registry, which I expected to be lowest because it is document-facing,
came in at 61%: its extrinsic citations are real but they are a minority of its
lines.

TWENTY STALE OR FALSE CLAIMS, every one verified before counting. NINE of the
first twelve were COUNTS. The full set adds eight more from pkg/cmd/export,
including: "diff 718 KB by hand" when the store is 891,499 bytes; "24 dead links"
when it composes 37 over 36 pages; "exactly one user" when there are two;
"fundFlowsCaveats returns three" when it returns two on one branch, added a day
after the comment. And data.go's "a one-method interface" for project.Labels,
which has three -- WITH THE SAME FALSE COUNT IN THE INTERFACE'S OWN DOC at
sankey.go:141. That is fisc-xbd4 exactly.

ONE OF THE TWENTY IS A FALSE CLAIM ABOUT A GUARD: data.go:477 says jscheck pins
"the figures in these comments". Re-measured through the harness: it does not pin
the sub-pixel counts. They are true and unguarded -- prose asserting a guard that
does not cover it, which is the green-because-the-gate-fired shape one level up.

41 DUPLICATE PAIRS. Worst: the internal/export-must-not-import-internal/project
layering rule appears three times in pkg/cmd/export; the resolution-path fact
four times in facts.go; the published-vs-derived invariant in TEN comment blocks
in internal/registry; the gutter definition four times in a 121-line file plus a
fifth copy in another package.

THE ERROR-STRING THESIS, TEMPERED. I reported it as the single largest confound.
The scorers put it at about half: in leaf-b only 2 of 4 message-adjacent comments
were second copies; in registry 12 of 13 were, but the operative rule is that the
comment earns its lines when it adds the CONSEQUENCE and not when it paraphrases
the string. In pkg/cmd/export three comments are second copies of an error string
1-3 lines below them. Real, and about half, not all.

CALIBRATION. I scored 24 of pkg/cmd/export's 87 target blocks by hand and got 49%
droppable; the agent scoring all 87 got 42%. Seven points apart, my sample the
optimistic one. That is the only inter-rater check available and it is reassuring
about direction, not about the second digit.

THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT RESULT is not a percentage. registry.go:365's doc
comment states a distinction that, when stripped, caused a careful reader to
conclude in writing that Assignable "defaults to TRUE at load and FALSE at query"
-- a false claim about a permission flag, confidently made and line-cited. That
is a comment whose absence produced a measurable error, which is the strongest
evidence this method can generate, and it is worth more than any RECOVERED count.

WHAT A SWEEP SHOULD DO WITH THIS.
  - Exported: do not delete. Fix the 21 UNDER-DOCUMENTED first; they are the ones
    that can cause a bug at a call site.
  - Unexported/inline: about half the lines can go, and the safe method is
    delete-then-restore-VERBATIM, never paraphrase -- fisc-pm8f measured ~2 new
    false claims per 10 hand-rewritten blocks.
  - The 41 duplicate pairs are the cheapest win and need no judgement: pick the
    home, delete the copies.
  - The 20 stale claims are filed as fisc-gyg9 and are worth fixing regardless of
    whether any sweep happens.
================= PEER REVIEW OF THE MEASUREMENT ITSELF =====================

Two independent checks were run on this audit's own output. Both were worth it
and one of them significantly changes what may be claimed.

1. INTER-RATER RELIABILITY. 32 target blocks drawn at random across all four
   packages, re-scored from scratch by a second rater who saw the same blocks,
   the same blind account and the same rubric, and was NOT shown the first
   rater's verdicts.

     headline (droppable % of lines)   rater 1: 55%   rater 2: 53%   GAP 2 POINTS
     exact verdict agreement           22/32 = 69%   Cohen's kappa 0.50
     collapsed, fully-droppable vs earns-something   27/32 = 84%
     blocks disagreeing by more than 2 lines         1 of 32

   THE FAILURE MODE IS THE RIGHT ONE. Six of the ten disagreements are
   PARTIAL vs MISSED-REASONING -- a taxonomy boundary, not a reading difference.
   The raters disagree about what to CALL a block and agree about how many of its
   lines earn their place, which is what the number is computed from. So the 51%
   is credible to within a few points; the four-category taxonomy is not
   reproducible enough to quote per-category rates.

2. ADVERSARIAL REVIEW OF THE STALE CLAIMS. A reviewer was told to REFUTE the
   twenty, default to "the accusation is wrong", and redo every measurement
   rather than accept mine.

     CONFIRMED 12    PARTLY 6    REFUTED 2

   EIGHT OF TWENTY FAILED. Full detail is on fisc-gyg9. The two outright
   refutations were mine misreading scope: a comment that says "until now no
   Builder could reach it" was accused of a count the same commit updates, and a
   comment that says the checks "re-measure" was accused of claiming they "pin".

   AND ONE OF THE EIGHT IS ONE I PERSONALLY VERIFIED AND REPORTED AS CONFIRMED.
   path.go:53 was called an invented citation, false the day it was written, on
   the strength of `git log --all -S "--output site"`. The same invocation is
   spelled `fisc export -o site` in four committed places, and the sibling test
   says "which this command's Example ONCE suggested". A one-spelling grep, in a
   session whose entire subject is one-spelling greps.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE HEADLINE. The 51% is unaffected -- it comes from the
verdicts, which replicated to within 2 points. What it damages is the STALE
LIST, which was the audit's other product: 12 of 20 stand, and one of those needs
its own number corrected (project.Labels has six methods, not the three both
scorers said and not the one the comment says).

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the reusable part. Every check in this audit that
COMPUTED something replicated. Every check that ASSERTED something about the tree
had roughly a 40% failure rate until attacked, INCLUDING the ones done by hand
and reported as verified. A blind-read oracle is good at producing candidates and
bad at confirming them, and the confirming step needs an adversary rather than a
second look from the same direction.
=========== FOLLOW-UP EXPERIMENT: FABLE REWRITES A FILE TO THE SHAPE ==========

QUESTION. fisc-pm8f measured that hand-editing comments manufactures roughly two
new false claims per ten blocks. Does a from-scratch rewrite by a different model,
given only the written rules and the original text, do better?

SETUP. internal/geom/{geom.go,grid.go} -- 28 blocks, 147 comment lines, 84% of
them exported docs. Chosen because it contained a KNOWN FALSE CLAIM ("the CIP is
landscape") and a known duplicate, neither disclosed. Inputs: AGENTS.md's own
rules extracted verbatim, plus the exported/unexported distinction, plus the
files. NOT given: the audit's verdicts, the stale list, or any finding.
Metrics were pre-registered before the run. The repo was never the working copy.

RESULT, against the four pre-registered metrics.

1. NEW FALSE CLAIMS: ZERO. Every new or altered factual assertion checked
   independently -- the corrected orientation figures (CIP 248/75, ACFR 174/21,
   Budget Book 268/0); "786 artifacts, zero violations" (reimplemented the five
   checks in a scan: 786/0); "shares no memory with p.Words" (newLine does
   slices.Clone); "Band panics outside [0, Len())" (bare slice index). All true.
   ONE INCOMPLETENESS: ParsePage's new refusal enumeration omits the JSON-decode
   failure, which is the case a caller most often hits. Incomplete, not false.

   Against ~2 per 10 blocks for incremental hand-editing, over 28 blocks.

2. IT FOUND THE PLANTED FALSE CLAIM UNAIDED and corrected it rather than
   propagating it, having measured the orientation split itself. That was the
   experiment's main probe.

3. VOLUME: 147 -> 131 lines, -11%. The audit's ceiling for this file was 14%
   droppable. So it captured about four fifths of the available slack and stopped
   near where an independent oracle said to stop.

4. ALIGNMENT WITH THE AUDIT, WHICH IT NEVER SAW, is the strongest signal:
     - the ONE fully-RECOVERED block in the file was DELETED outright;
     - the CONTRADICTED block was CORRECTED, growing by a line;
     - the UNDER-DOCUMENTED block (Band) GAINED its missing contract;
     - all five PARTIAL blocks were trimmed, each in the right direction;
     - most SUFFICIENT exported docs were left alone.

IT ALSO EXPOSED A FLAW IN MY OWN RUBRIC, which is the more useful outcome.
Eight of its sixteen cut lines came out of blocks the audit scored SUFFICIENT --
Right's "named so that the filing rule reads as prose at its call site",
Height's "the quantity Page.Lines derives its clustering tolerance from". Both
are symbol-locating restatements that rule 1 excludes, and both were invisible to
the audit BECAUSE MY SCORING SET earns = lines FOR EVERY SUFFICIENT BLOCK. The
rubric conflates "a consumer can use this" with "not one line is surplus", and
therefore cannot see padding inside an adequate doc. The 51% headline is
consequently a FLOOR on the exported side too, not only on the internal side.

WHAT IT LOST, and this is the honest cost. Three consequence chains went:
the ghost-word chain (a null coordinate "passes the inverted-box check, sorts to
the front of the page, anchors the first line cluster, and drags the median word
height down" -> "a zero-area ghost word at the page origin"); newLine's
"a consumer comparing this line against the page text token by token would
disagree on exactly the jittered lines the tolerance was for"; and
SchemaVersion's "a reader pinned to the wrong one would report a perfectly good
page as unreadable". Each compresses a WHY-IT-MATTERS into a WHAT-IT-IS. All
three are defensible under the rules and all three are, to my reading, slightly
over-trimmed -- the consequence is what makes a guard's importance legible.

CONCLUSION. The desired shape is reachable by rewriting, and rewriting is SAFER
than incremental hand-editing rather than more dangerous, which inverts the
assumption behind the delete-and-restore-verbatim recommendation. The residual
risk is not false claims; it is over-compression of the reasoning that justifies
a guard. A sweep should therefore ask for the consequence to be KEPT explicitly,
and should still verify: one enumeration came back incomplete.
close_reason: COMPLETE, and its central recommendation was refuted by its own follow-up. The measurement landed: 343 blocks, 1,826 lines, 8 packages -- 51% of unexported/inline comment lines recoverable from the code, 6% of exported doc lines, and 21 exported docs UNDER-documented. Peer-reviewed: the 51% replicated to within 2 points by a blind second rater, while 8 of the 20 stale claims did not survive an adversary, including one verified by hand and reported confirmed. THE RECOMMENDATION IS WITHDRAWN: 'the safe method is delete-then-restore-VERBATIM, never paraphrase' was inverted by this bead's own Fable experiment (aa9ada7), which rewrote a file from scratch with zero new false claims. And the rewrite direction that followed is now priced and declined -- see fisc-b93j. What survives and is still true: the exported/unexported standards differ by roughly 8x, the API needs MORE prose and the internals less, and the strongest single result is registry.go:365, a comment whose absence produced a measurable false inference about a permission flag. Successors: fisc-a3rp, fisc-jbu4, fisc-mwne, fisc-ynuo, fisc-jnuf.

title: A comment names a symbol; it does not restate, locate, or count
description:
A comment names a symbol; it does not restate what the symbol does, where it
lives, or how many of anything there are. Two rules plus a history corollary,
into AGENTS.md, then a three-lane sweep.

WHY, MEASURED. The 2026-08-31 session classified 115 findings; prose held 32
(PROSE-NEW 20, PROSE-PRE-EXISTING 12) and FALSE-CLAIM was 32 by kind. The
question asked afterwards was whether the cause is a narrative comment style
describing development history. IT IS NOT. History-marker comment lines are 247
of 18,746 (1.3%), and reclassifying the lanes' false-text instances by cause
gives: rule-restated-that-changed-elsewhere 35%, never-true-when-written 23%,
number-drifted 22%, history 15% -- and most of that 15% is a file rename
(drilldown.html), not narration.

The real cause is that almost every false claim was A SECOND COPY of a fact
whose home is elsewhere. The narrative register is the carrier, not the cause.

TWO THINGS THE ORIGINAL TAXONOMY HID:
  - The largest bucket is not comments. 22 of 65 false-text instances were
    user-facing or operator strings -- caveat text, ledes, <title>/<desc>,
    refusal messages. Filed WRONG-OUTPUT, so "prose = 32 of 115" undercounts by
    roughly half. unprojectedScopes' three reasons alone carry 106 hand-typed
    numbers, printed verbatim on every fisc verify run.
  - Duplication is the multiplier, which fisc-xbd4 already priced at one review
    pass per copy.

MEASURED AT 823de73:
  second-source surface
    production Go comments naming another file            159
    comments naming an exported symbol from another pkg   173
    comment mentions of a check id defined elsewhere      ~96 of 188
    comment references to a .go path                      102 (33 as "X in path")
    comment references to a data/artifact path            273  (these STAY)
    hand-typed numbers in strings fisc verify prints      204 over 8 files
                                                          = 45 page cites,
                                                            49 dollar citations,
                                                            69 bare counts
    ten corpus facts (924 786 231 312 196 88 78 61 23 247) 168 hits, mean 9 files
  narrative residue
    Go comment lines            18,746 of 62,341 (30%); non-test 10,962 of 27,673 (40%)
    history-register lines      247
    comments correcting an earlier version of themselves  24 across 22 files
    "Found by /code-review" credit lines in source        26 across 13 files
    "Measured" claims in Go comments                      85, of which 2 name a commit
    intrinsic count phrases in Go comments                ~85

THE RULES, verbatim, for AGENTS.md's existing "Comments are checkable claims"
and "Before you quote a number" -- not a new section, because that file's own
opening says overlapping copies of a rule are the failure it was merged to end.

  1. A comment names a symbol. It does not say what the symbol does, and it does
     not say where the symbol lives. Both are second sources nothing keeps in
     step: the edit that falsifies a restatement is in the other file, so its
     author never sees it, and a path goes stale the moment the symbol moves. Go
     tooling finds a symbol from its bare name -- qualify with a package only
     where the name is ambiguous.

     THE EXCEPTION IS SURPRISE. Document another API only where it does not make
     sense on its face, or has to be used oddly for this code to work -- and then
     write down WHAT SURPRISED YOU, not what the API does. That is the one thing
     the other file cannot tell the reader.

     DATA AND ARTIFACT PATHS ARE NOT SYMBOLS AND STAY: data/funds.yaml,
     testdata/pages/p0067.txt, mappings/*.yaml, site/app.js. Nothing to look up
     by name, so the path is the reference rather than a copy of one.

  2. Do not report a count of the tree's own contents. How many facts, nodes,
     links, subjects, checks or rules there are goes stale on the next commit and
     tells a reader nothing they could not get by looking. A count earns its
     place only when EXTRINSIC -- when it says something about a world outside
     the code that the code cannot report. "We handle 18 of the 20 status codes"
     is worth writing; "this returns 61 nodes" is not.

     Two kinds qualify and nothing else does:
       - A count against the documents. "pp.85-125's 78 rows", "23 divisions
         under 11 departments", "the corpus is 786 pages and the site cites 21".
         This is the project's subject and it stays.
       - A count that IS the evidence for a decision -- the reconciliation
         arithmetic, and app.js's 195 crossings against 285 / 297 / 246 under
         every other reachable ordering. It stays, and must be pinned by
         something that re-measures it, which is what layout.mjs exists for.

  3. (corollary) History's home is git. Delete the "Found by /code-review"
     credit lines from source -- AGENTS.md already puts that credit in the commit
     body. Delete the errata ("an earlier version of this comment said X"): they
     add a second claim, about the past, that nothing can check.

THE TESTS HERE ALREADY APPLY RULE 2 AND THE PROSE NEVER GOT THE MEMO.
TestTheCommittedCorpusVacuitySplit: "It asserts the words and not the subject
counts. The counts move with every page that gets mapped, and pinning them here
would make this a test of the mapping's size."
TestUnprojectedScopesAreDeclarations: "The count is deliberately NOT pinned."
Both refuse a count that ~85 comment phrases and 69 printed-string counts state.

TWO CONFIRMED LIVE DEFECTS, both second copies:
  - checks_test.go's doc comment on TestAStaleUnprojectedScopeDeclarationFails
    says transfersDetailScope is "the only entry left in the map".
    unprojectedScopes holds THREE, and a correct comment 30 lines above in the
    same file says "Three scopes are decided."
  - page.go's markZeroRadius and markMinBar carry the same ~60-word measurement
    paragraph, twice, on adjacent constants.

THE SWEEP, three commits and not one, because the loop is its own second-largest
defect source (27 of 115) and decay is what a shrinking fix commit looks like.

  LANE 1 -- narrative residue. Delete the 26 credit lines; collapse the 24
  self-corrections to the corrected statement (keep the RULE where an erratum
  carries one, e.g. parse.go's "No line numbers here on purpose"); fix the two
  live defects. One review pass: deletions of unverifiable text, no design
  surface. OUT OF SCOPE: AGENTS.md's own "(Correction, recorded here rather than
  by amending, because the log is the audit trail)" blocks stay -- the file
  argues for keeping them and that argument was never made for source comments.

  LANE 2 -- restatements and intrinsic counts. Densest first: internal/check
  (fundingsources, coverage, graph, nodetiers, rowfunds, subject, check,
  documents, transfersdetail), then sankey.go, page.go, data.go. Per comment,
  one of: DELETE / REDUCE TO A BARE SYMBOL / KEEP AS SURPRISE -- and say which in
  the commit body. Calibrate on fundingSourcesTiesToSpine's doc comment: 65
  lines, the longest in the tree, ~45 of them describing what netCells,
  fact-departments-resolve, row-funds-match-their-anchors and
  rule-funds-match-their-headings do. What survives is the surprise -- that these
  rows carry no department is a CONSTRAINT, because fact-departments-resolve
  resolves against a division, so typing one reddens six of eleven rules -- plus
  the reconciliation arithmetic, which is this check's own evidence. Test
  comments included; rowfunds_test.go's TestRowFundsCatchesABareLabelTwinTheGate-
  DoesNot is the densest single instance, a 23-line block quoting a sha and four
  verify pass counts, two unpinned, none asserted by its own test.

  LANE 3 -- printed strings. Page cites and dollar figures are extrinsic
  citations: verify against facts.jsonl and data/extracted/, then leave. The 69
  bare counts take rule 2 -- delegate to the check whose summary already prints
  it (the pattern unprojectedScopes' own reason text already uses: "its own
  summary line carries the count, which is why one is not repeated here"), or
  compute from the Subject, as 9c85d73 did when it made the caveat figures
  computed rather than literal.

  Safe: nothing pins these strings. TestUnprojectedScopesAreDeclarations checks
  shape only (non-empty, no two reasons byte-identical, cites a page or bead);
  no golden holds verify output. Keep the no-duplicate-reason property.
  facts.jsonl must not move.

EXPECT FEW CORRECTIONS AND MANY DELETIONS. Spot-checked and correct today: every
unprojectedScopes scope count (88/924/312/196/240/20 against facts.jsonl), 786
extracted pages, 61 tier-3 fund nodes, 247 nodes carrying a constraint_tier. All
four are INTRINSIC and all four go -- which is the point. They are right, and a
copy of one still cost a review pass every time it drifted.

VERIFICATION. make pre-commit; make js; rebuild bin/fisc and read the check count
off THAT run; fisc build --output bin/facts-rebuilt.jsonl and cmp against
facts/facts.jsonl. Lane 3 additionally diffs fisc verify output before and after:
a count that vanished without a computing check taking it over is a coverage
claim quietly withdrawn. Review per the loop, three passes minimum and five at
most, stopping on no WRONG-OUTPUT and no FAIL-OPEN.
notes:
RE-DERIVED AT e3ebc7a, 2026-09-02. Both premises hold: the tree is byte-identical
to the measurement commit 823de73 for every code file (git diff --stat

  claim                                    exact-phrase grep    broad grep
  26 credit lines across 13 files          20 / 14 files        37
  24 self-corrections across 22 files      15 / 14 files        35 / 25 files
  102 comment refs to a .go path           78 (47 non-test)     --
  ...33 of them in the "X in path" form    7                    --

SESSION 2026-09-02: LANE 1 COMPLETE, LANE 2 PARTIAL AND AT THE FIVE-PASS CAP.
Nine commits, dfc4033..178e8ba. Lane 3 not started.

LANDED

           sections, and this bead's two corrections
  5dcc16b  lane 1: 66 credit lines across 28 files, the prose errata, and the

  7618d7b  lane 2 pass A: 14 .go-path references reduced to bare symbols

  dca0da0 / e71b037 / c186c82 / 324de61 / 178e8ba

WHAT LANE 2 DID NOT DO, and this is the larger half. The restatement sweep

description:

Populate applies_to only where it is HONEST: internal-service-charges -> fund-group/internal-service, contested-total-* -> its group, the transfers caveat -> transfers/in and transfers/out. Working-capital and permanent-funds are document-wide and correctly carry an EMPTY list -- which is why empty means document-wide rather than not-filled-in-yet.

TWO THINGS THIS STEP AND ONLY THIS STEP FORCES:

(1) schema_version must go to 2, or drawableSankey needs an arm. The badge makes the client dereference projection.metadata.caveats[].applies_to from a LAZILY FETCHED, UNCACHED document (app.js:1639) -- the exact stale-copy scenario drawableSankey's doc comment enumerates. A bump costs project.SchemaVersion, export.SchemaVersion, app.js:155, both goldens, and the fixtures at views_test.go:57, export_test.go:496/538/586/588/721, harness.mjs:383/590, fold.mjs:34.

(2) applies_to MUST SURVIVE THE FOLD or the badge silently never appears. foldDocument rewrites tier-3 and tier-5 nodes onto ancestors, so a caveat naming a fund id matches no DRAWN node. Either restrict applies_to to ids that survive the declared tiers, or have pin() resolve through the same ancestor map the fold built. THIS IS A GREEN-BECAUSE-THE-GATE-FIRED SHAPE: a test asserting 'no badge' passes either way.

Consider a caveat-targets-resolve check (ids unique per document; every applies_to names a node the document carries). That is the separate five-edit path -- new file, check.go registry, subject_test.go want map, checks_test.go counts AND the separate lenient.Counts.Vacuous assertion.
notes:
CORRECTION to this bead's close reason, recorded here rather than by amending: it argued the schema bump was avoidable because 'lifecycle.mjs drives it', meaning a drawableSankey arm for metadata.caveats[].applies_to. THAT ARM WAS REMOVED IN 25322d3 and the argument with it.

The arm was wrong for a reason its own justification made checkable: drawableSankey refuses a document over every key the draw DEREFERENCES, and caveatsFor dereferences neither -- it tests Array.isArray and returns []. So the arm refused a whole chart over a key whose absence costs a BADGE, and a reader with a cached pre-caveats document got a banner instead of a chart minus one chip.

WHAT IS TRUE NOW: no bump and no arm. The guarded dereference IS the degradation, and it is the right one. A stale document draws its chart and shows no caveat chips, which is what a reader of a pre-caveats file should get.
close_reason:
Landed. The fold hazard the bead named was real and is the whole of the work: caveatsFor resolves through the hierarchy, so a caveat naming fund/100 marks that node on spending.html and fund-group/general on revenue.html, where it folds. Mutation-verified -- direct id matching leaves revenue.html silent while spending.html still works, which is the shape an assertion about absence cannot detect.

THE SCHEMA BUMP WAS NOT NEEDED. The bead offered a bump or a drawableSankey arm; the arm costs one condition and refuses a stale document BY NAME, where a bump would refuse the same documents and cost two Go constants, app.js, both goldens and eight fixtures. lifecycle.mjs drives it, so the cheaper choice is the checked one.

WHAT THE BEAD DID NOT ANTICIPATE: columnShare needs the LAID nodes rather than the projection, because which column a mark is in is d3-sankey's answer and not the file's. And only ONE caveat in the corpus names a node worth marking -- the constraint-tier one is on every fund in the column, so marking all 61 marks none.

title: transfer_out facts carry opposite signs in two documents, and Fact.Sign says positive in both
description:
FOUND 2026-08-30 by the second review pass over 0448a5b^..ae52915, in text that DESCRIBED the hazard in two committed files and filed nothing. The description was written; the bead was not. That is the failure mode AGENTS.md names by name, and it is why this exists.

THE ASYMMETRY. Budget Book p66 prints TRANSFER OUT as a POSITIVE magnitude in a uses column: general FY2026-27 is 10,146,598. ACFR p41 prints Transfers (out) PARENTHESISED, because its block sums to a net Other Financing Sources (Uses): (25.72) million, published as -2,572,000,000 cents.

Both are correct as published -- 'AmountCents is always the figure as the document printed it' is the invariant, and neither document is being misread. The consequence is that summing transfer_out across scopes gives nonsense, and a consumer has no way to know.

AND Fact.Sign CANNOT TELL THEM APART, which is the part that makes this a bug rather than a note. Sign is the one field whose job is to say how a row relates to its category, and BOTH conventions carry sign: positive. Its doc comment says a contra row 'arrives here already negative' and that sign is 'NOT an instruction to negate' -- fine for Budget Book p127's ERAF, which is a deduction inside its own category. The ACFR case is different in kind: it is not a deduction, it is the same quantity with the opposite orientation, and Sign has no member for that. The comment even anticipates the shape: 'If a document ever prints a deduction as a positive number under a "Less:" heading, that convention needs its own field rather than an overload of this one.' This is that sentence's mirror image.

NOTHING IN internal/check SEES IT, measured. The two scopes (all-funds-gross and acfr-general-fund-summary) share no (kind, category, fund_group, fund, fiscal year, basis) key -- different year, different basis -- so projection-scopes-are-disjoint has nothing to compare; no detail-ties-to-spine check spans them and none can; and fact-kind-matches-category is satisfied by both, since transfers/out declares kind transfer_out and says nothing about orientation. fisc verify is 41 passed, 0 failed with both conventions in the store.

WHY IT IS NOT URGENT AND IS STILL REAL: today exactly ONE fact carries the ACFR convention, it is in an unprojected scope, and no published view sums across the two. It becomes real the moment a second ACFR block lands or anything aggregates transfer_out corpus-wide.

WHERE IT IS DESCRIBED TODAY: mappings/livermore-acfr-fy2025.yaml's header note ('A NOTE ON SIGN'), and the transfers/out alias note in data/taxonomy.yaml. Both should cite this bead rather than trailing off.

OPTIONS, none free:
  (a) a new Sign member -- e.g. SignNetted or SignOriented -- saying the document prints this row with the opposite orientation to its kind's convention. Honest, and it makes the distinction stateable rather than inferable.
  (b) normalise on the way in, so every transfer_out is a positive magnitude. REFUSED unless argued hard: it breaks 'nothing re-signs a value between the parser and this record', and the token would then disagree with amount_cents in sign, which fact-token-reparses would catch and which is the point of that check.
  (c) leave it, and require any consumer summing across scopes to say which convention it assumes.
acceptance_criteria: either a fact record states which sign convention its document uses and a check can fail on a consumer that mixes them, or the two documents' transfer_out orientation is reconciled without re-signing any published figure; the rule file and the taxonomy alias note cite the outcome
close_reason: Option (a) taken: mapping.SignNetted, declared on ACFR p41's Transfers (out) row, plus fact-transfer-orientation-is-declared to make it non-optional. Option (b) stays refused -- nothing is re-signed, amount_cents is still -2572000000, exactly the token the page prints -- and option (c) would not have met this bead's own acceptance clause, which asks for a check. Sign is NOT in MakeID's hashed tuple, so the change moves one field on one fact and every id is stable: facts.jsonl is one line, sign positive -> netted. The check is restricted to transfer_in/transfer_out on purpose, and the restriction is pinned by two of its six test cases: the store carries 16 negative facts, and 15 of them are legitimate magnitudes -- p127's '(20,033)' Prior Year - Unsecured revenue and six spine fund_balance lines that fell -- so 'a negative amount must be declared' would have reddened all of them. Proven failable end to end: removing sign: netted and rebuilding takes verify from 44 passed 0 failed to 43 passed 1 FAILED, naming fisc-f-37ee25c212bb. Both texts that described the hazard now cite the outcome -- the rule file's A NOTE ON SIGN and data/taxonomy.yaml's transfers/out alias -- and both state the residue plainly: this buys legibility, not protection. Nothing stops a consumer summing across conventions; when a projection selects acfr-general-fund-summary, the check that refuses the mixture now has a field to read.

title: A figure printed between a block's last row and its total can be neither declared nor omitted
description:
FOUND 2026-08-30 mapping ACFR p41 (fisc-9hf). It is what keeps that page's revenue block unmapped.

THE PAGE. data/extracted/livermore-acfr-fy2025/pages/p0041.txt line 27 is a bare '0.0' on a line of its own, sitting between the Miscellaneous row's figures and the Total Revenues row. It is in the FY2024 column and belongs to no printed row label -- an artefact of the city's spreadsheet, not a row.

EVERY EXIT IS CLOSED, and this was traced rather than assumed:
  - labelledValues' trailing arm (internal/mapping/resolve.go:518) refuses it: '"0.0" follows the last mapped row but is not mapped'.
  - stop_at cannot name it. validateRule (internal/mapping/parse.go) refuses a section or stop_at anchor that amount.Parse accepts, correctly -- anchoring a block on a figure is circular. Normalize trims whitespace before parsing, so no padded spelling escapes it.
  - An eleventh {label: "0.0", skip: true} row fails the len(toks) < ncols guard, because the block ends immediately after it.
  - wrapped_labels IS mechanically accepted and is a FALSE CLAIM: it asserts the page wrapped a LABEL onto its own line. This is a figure. The stale-wrapped_labels arm exists precisely to stop declarations that are not true of the document.

So the honest state is that the block cannot be read, and it is not read. TestACFRp0041RevenueBlockCannotBeResolved asserts both the orphan's presence and its position between the last row and the printed total, so if the page changes the test says so.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT: a Part declaration for unmapped non-label text -- something like unmapped_text: [{text: "0.0", note: "..."}] -- modelled on StatedTotalDelta rather than on wrapped_labels. The point of that model is that it is a claim with a required reason that FAILS when it stops being true: a declared fragment the page no longer prints must go red, exactly as a declared delta that now ties exactly does. A silent skip would be the wrong shape.

NOTE THE SECOND BLOCKER. Even with this resolved, ACFR p41's revenue block still cannot be read: its first row prints a STANDALONE '$' before each figure ('$       60.42    $        57.70'), which is fisc-yun, the same shape that makes ACFR p177 unreadable. Both are asserted on the page by the test named above. Fixing this bead alone does not make the block mappable.
acceptance_criteria: a figure printed inside a block and belonging to no row can be declared with a required reason; the declaration fails when the page stops printing it; ACFR p41's revenue block is readable to the extent fisc-yun allows
notes:
2026-08-30 THE 'SECOND BLOCKER' PARAGRAPH IN THIS BEAD'S DESCRIPTION IS FALSE, AND SO IS ITS ACCEPTANCE CRITERION. Corrected here rather than by rewriting them, because this bead was filed in the same session that got it wrong and the record of the mistake is worth more than a clean description.

WHAT THE DESCRIPTION SAYS: 'NOTE THE SECOND BLOCKER. Even with this resolved, ACFR p41's revenue block still cannot be read: its first row prints a STANDALONE $ before each figure, which is fisc-yun ... Fixing this bead alone does not make the block mappable.' The acceptance criterion says '...readable to the extent fisc-yun allows'.

MEASURED, by building the revenue rule and running it (not by reading the page):

  Values REFUSED: livermore-acfr-fy2025 p41: rule "probe": rows: "0.0" follows
  the last mapped row but is not mapped

That is the ONLY refusal. All ten rows read, including the one with the standalone marks. fisc-yun is CLOSED -- dropCurrencyMarks (internal/mapping/resolve.go) drops a token that is a currency mark and nothing else, in exactly the labelled read this rule uses. The claim came from a bead title rather than from the tree.

SO THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION SHOULD READ: a figure printed inside a block and belonging to no row can be declared with a required reason; the declaration fails when the page stops printing it; and ACFR p41's revenue block then RESOLVES -- with nothing else in the way.

THE SAME WRONG CLAIM WAS CORRECTED IN FOUR OTHER PLACES in the same lane: mappings/livermore-acfr-fy2025.yaml, internal/check/coverage.go's unprojectedScopes entry (which fisc verify prints on every run, and which now says 'that orphan is the ONLY blocker'), testdata/README.md's p41 row, and testdata/README.md's p177 row, where the same false 'live fisc-yun' claim had been committed earlier and independently.

ALSO STALE: the description's account of what TestACFRp0041RevenueBlockCannotBeResolved asserts. That test no longer asserts things about the page text -- it RUNS the rule and requires the refusal to name the orphan, precisely so a claim like the one above cannot survive in it again.
close_reason: Landed at d9a5b80 as Part.UnmappedText, and the bead's own premise turned out to be FALSE, which is the more useful half of the result. It said the orphan 'can be neither declared nor omitted'; measured before changing anything, wrapped_labels: ["0.0"] parsed, resolved all ten of ACFR p41's revenue rows and tied to the printed total with nothing objecting. The honesty rule was an instruction in a comment, not a check. So this landed as TWO changes: unmapped_text, a declaration with a required note and its own staleness arm that must PARSE as an amount; and the mirror refusal that a wrapped_labels entry must NOT. Neither can now stand in for the other. All five committed wrapped_labels entries are refused by amount.Parse, so the new refusal costs the corpus nothing. p41's revenue block is published, ten rows tying to 157.20 exactly. Left open and filed: fisc-0cff, the same shape one gap earlier -- a figure before a block's FIRST row is still undeclarable, because wiring unmapped_text into the leading arm would retire the only guard that gap has.

title: Two rules over one section can publish the same printed figure twice, and every check stays green
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-30 while landing mappings/livermore-acfr-fy2025.yaml (fisc-9hf).

THE SHAPE. ACFR p41 is read by two rules over the SAME section anchor: acfr-p0041-gf-other-financing-sources publishes the two transfer rows, and acfr-p0041-gf-fund-balances declares those same three lines skip: true so their figures are consumed rather than left as unexplained text between rows. That is the only way to reach the fund-balance rows below them, because checkGap refuses undeclared text between rows and a value-bearing line cannot go in wrapped_labels.

THE HOLE. Give one of those skipped rows a category and a MATCHING kind instead of skip: true, rebuild, and the store publishes the page's single printed 0.53 twice -- 106,000,000 cents of ACFR transfers/in where p41 prints 53,000,000. Measured: fisc verify --strict reports 40 passed, 0 failed.

WHY NOTHING SEES IT:
  - fact.MakeID hashes rule_id, so the two facts have different ids and CheckUniqueIDs is satisfied;
  - both re-parse their own token (fact-token-reparses) and both offsets land on that token (fact-offset-points-at-token), because it IS the same printed figure;
  - no detail-ties-to-spine check applies -- acfr-general-fund-summary has no spine counterpart and cannot have one (FY2025 audited against a spine that prints no audited column);
  - projection-scopes-are-disjoint compares scopes, and both facts are in the same scope.

It goes red only on a MISMATCHED kind, via fact-kind-matches-category, which catches the kind and not the doubling. That is the 'green because the gate fired' shape AGENTS.md names.

NOT A DEFECT IN WHAT SHIPPED -- the committed rules declare the skips correctly, and the rule file's note records the measurement. It is an unguarded hazard that this lane introduced, and the first time two rules have shared one section in this corpus.

WHAT A FIX HAS TO HANDLE: p76 legitimately publishes TWO facts from one printed figure (the two legs of a transfer, both citing the same doc_id/page/offset), so a naive 'no two facts share (doc_id, page, offset)' check would redden 88 committed facts. The distinction is that p76's second leg is a DECLARED counterpart. So the check is something like: two facts sharing (doc_id, page, offset) must be a row and its declared counterpart, and anything else is a double-publish.
acceptance_criteria: two rules publishing the same (doc_id, page, offset) without a declared counterpart makes fisc verify fail; the p76 counterpart legs stay green; proven by mutating a skip: true row in mappings/livermore-acfr-fy2025.yaml
close_reason: fact-citations-are-declared landed. Two facts may cite one (doc_id, page, offset) only as ONE rule's ONE row with a declared Counterpart; anything else is a finding. The 44 addresses p76 legitimately shares -- 88 of the committed facts, every pair the same rule_id and row_label differing only in kind, row_path and column_path -- stay green, which a rule refusing every shared citation would not have. Proven end to end by the mutation the rule file itself describes: turning the ACFR p41 'Transfers in' skip:true row into a published row rebuilds a store where two DIFFERENT rules cite p41's single printed 0.53, and verify goes 43 passed 0 failed -> 42 passed 1 FAILED with the finding naming both rules and the token. It was 0 failed before this check. Also five table cases in TestOnePrintedFigureIsTwoFactsOnlyWhenARowDeclaresIt, each proven failable: neutering declaresCounterpart reddens the undeclared-row case, and removing the two-rules arm reddens the ACFR case. The rule file's 'NOTHING GUARDS THEM' paragraph was corrected in the same commit.

title: TestCIPp40SparseRowFailsClosedButDoesNotRead is green because a different gate fired
description:
internal/mapping/geometry_test.go:717. The test's doc comment claims it proves 'the read fails, and it fails naming the row rather than filing the second 550,000 under a year the city never put it in'. It proves neither.

MEASURED (throwaway test in internal/mapping, 2026-08-29). res.Values(rule, part) for cipRule(t, 40, "PROJECT NAME", "TOTAL - PARKS", "PB200654") fails with:

  livermore-cip-fy2026-2030 p40: rule "cip": section: figures appear before the first row "PB200654": "FY 2024-25  FY 2025-26 ... PB200429 Rehabilitation ... PB200646 LARPD Park Expansion Projects ..."
  hint: the block starts too early -- move the section anchor past the column headers

That is checkGap's LEADING-GAP arm. The block starts at the column headers, so the resolver refuses before it ever reaches PB200654's row read. The test's only assertion, strings.Contains(diagnosis, "PB200654"), is satisfied incidentally because the leading-gap message quotes the first row's ANCHOR NAME. So the assertion passes on an error that has nothing to do with the sparse row.

WHY IT MATTERS: this test is cited as the evidence for fisc-8ln's interim-state paragraph and was, until this session, the basis for AGENTS.md's account of what labelledValues does on a sparse row. Two successive attempts to summarise that mechanism in AGENTS.md got it backwards (bcbc4fb, then dc831e2 corrected the correction) and this test could not have caught either, because it never exercises the code path.

This is the 'green because the gate fired' shape AGENTS.md names, and at least the fourth occurrence -- the others are jscheck's twoYearConfig docs:{}, the modelling-ids-not-attributes case, and the removeAttribute('disabled') case in harness.mjs.

THE FIX IS NOT TO LOOSEN THE ASSERTION. Move the section anchor past the column headers so the block starts at the first data row, then assert on the row read itself: the error must name PB200654 AND the column, and must arise from the row read rather than from checkGap. Prove it can fail -- with the anchor fixed, reverting the column guard should change the outcome; if it does not, the test still is not reaching the code it is named for.

Found by /code-review over bcbc4fb^..dc831e2.
close_reason:
Landed at 3302fb0. The test now reaches the row read.

WHAT WAS WRONG, exactly as the bead measured it: the section anchored on 'PROJECT NAME', the column-header line's own label, so the block began at the headers and checkGap's leading-gap arm refused before any row was read. The one assertion, Contains('PB200654'), passed on that message quoting the first row's ANCHOR NAME.

THE FIX THE BEAD ASKED FOR: 'Move the section anchor past the column headers so the block starts at the first data row, then assert on the row read itself.' Done -- the section is now the header line's trailing 'TOTAL' at ordinal 1 (the page's closing 'TOTAL - PARKS & BEAUTIFICATION' carries the word again), the rule declares the two rows above PB200654 so their figures are consumed rather than sitting in the leading gap, and PB200654's wrapped label gets a wrapped_labels entry. The read reaches the row and refuses with 'row PB200654 Holmes Street is followed by 2 values, want 8'.

TWO ASSERTIONS THE OLD TEST LACKED, and they are what make it falsifiable: the error must report the value count, and it must NOT be the leading-gap message. Restoring the old anchor reddens both.

THE BEAD'S SUGGESTED MUTATION PROOF DOES NOT WORK, AND THE REASON IS THE MORE USEFUL FINDING. It said 'with the anchor fixed, reverting the column guard should change the outcome; if it does not, the test still is not reaching the code it is named for.' Measured: it does not change the outcome, AND the test IS reaching the row. The row yields 2 tokens against 8 columns, so len(toks) < ncols refuses first and geometry never places anything -- the error is identical with column_headers declared and without. On this row the value count is the whole defence.

That guard is also load-bearing beyond a wrong read: neutering it does not mis-file the second 550,000, it PANICS on the toks[:ncols] two lines below -- 'slice bounds out of range [:8] with capacity 2'.

AGENTS.md carried the old claim ('fisc-i0d9 owns the separate fact that TestCIPp40SparseRowFailsClosedButDoesNotRead ... never reaches the row read') and is corrected with all of the above.

title: test-tempdir memory tells every session to avoid the committed testdata/ tree this repo depends on
description:
The injected memory 'test-tempdir' says: "Write fixtures inline with os.WriteFile rather than maintaining a committed testdata/ tree -- tests stay hermetic, parallel-safe, and the fixture and assertion read on the same screen."

AGENTS.md requires the opposite. Its Testing section says to use the fixtures in testdata/, which are REAL ARTIFACTS copied from data/extracted/, names testdata/README.md as required reading because every fixture exists for a specific named failure mode, and warns that a drifted fixture is the bad case because tests stay green against a substrate that no longer exists (fisc-yqv.5).

This is not a stale detail. It is an instruction, injected verbatim into every session by bd prime, telling a future agent to do the opposite of the house rule -- the class AGENTS.md calls a defect rather than cosmetics. The memory does carve out 'Reserve testdata/ for truly static reference files', which technically covers the 24+2 page fixtures, but a session reading the leading sentence acts on it.

FIX: append one clause in place naming this repo's exception. Do not forget the memory -- the generic advice is sound for tests that write their own scratch files, and pkg/cmdutil/atomic_test.go is a fair user of it.
close_reason: The clause landed in the same session the bead was filed. test-tempdir now opens its second paragraph with 'IN THIS REPO THE COMMITTED testdata/ TREE IS LOAD-BEARING AND THE EXCEPTION IS THE RULE', names the 24+2 page fixtures and the manifest sha256 requirement, cites fisc-yqv.5 for what a drifted fixture costs, and keeps t.TempDir() plus inline os.WriteFile as right for scratch-writing tests. Verified in the live memory, not from the plan. The bead was filed per 'Nothing leaves a pass unfiled' before the fix was written and would otherwise have sat in bd ready as already-done work quoting the pre-fix text in the present tense -- found by /code-review over bcbc4fb^..dc831e2.

title: A fact can name a department only if that department is also a division
description:
fact-departments-resolve (internal/check/vocabulary.go) resolves a fact's
`department:` against Vocabulary.Division, and check.Subject's Vocabulary
interface does not expose Department at all. data/departments.yaml lists 11
departments and 23 divisions, and SIX of the eleven are not division slugs:
library-department, innovation-and-economic-development, police-department,
community-development, public-works, fire-department.

So a fact whose natural department axis is the DEPARTMENT tier cannot carry one.
It is not that nobody typed it -- typing it makes the check red.

WHERE THIS BITES TODAY. pp.85-125's Department Funding Sources (fisc-71j, scope
department-funding-sources) is a per-department schedule and its 312 facts carry
`department: ""`. README describes it as "which funds pay for each department"
and the facts record no department; the department is recoverable only from
rule_id, which is a string no consumer parses. Every one of those facts also
shares one row_path, `department-funding-sources`, because RowPath falls back to
the category when there is no department.

AND IT COSTS A GUARD, which is the part worth fixing for rather than tidiness.
internal/project's netCells REFUSES a fact carrying a department outright --
that is what makes a mis-scoped pp.167-170 rule fail loudly rather than double
the General Fund silently. A funding-source fact carrying its department would
inherit that refusal, so `scope: all-funds-gross` on one of those rules would be
a build-time error instead of something only funding-sources-tie-to-spine sees.
internal/check/fundingsources.go's doc comment says as much and cannot act on it.

OPTIONS, none free:
  (a) let a fact name either tier -- add Department to check.Subject's
      Vocabulary and accept a department-tier slug, which weakens the check's
      current claim ("joins to nothing") into two claims and needs the
      projections to know which tier they are looking at;
  (b) add the six missing names as divisions of themselves, which is a lie
      about data/departments.yaml's own structure;
  (c) leave it, and say so in the taxonomy and the rule file rather than
      leaving a reader to discover it.

(c) is what fisc-71j shipped. Decide between (a) and (c) before fisc-7q6, which
maps the SAME fourteen pages at the division tier and will carry a department on
every row -- at which point the funding-source facts sitting beside them with a
blank one is a visible asymmetry rather than a quiet one.

Found by /code-review over cd1192c^..HEAD.
acceptance_criteria: either a funding-source fact carries its department and fisc verify stays green, or the taxonomy entry and the rule file both say why it cannot and name this bead
notes:
2026-09-03 THE PREMISE IS UNCHANGED AND TWO OF THIS BEAD'S FIGURES HAVE MOVED. Re-derived by the fifth review pass over the departmentwide lane.

WHAT IS STILL EXACTLY TRUE: fact-departments-resolve resolves against a DIVISION; six of the eleven departments are not division slugs; pp.85-125's 312 department-funding-sources facts still carry department: "" and still share one row_path; and netCells' refusal of a fact carrying a department is still a guard those facts do not get. Nothing here weakens the bead.

TWO NUMBERS: the file now lists 11 departments and TWENTY-NINE divisions, not 23. The departmentwide lane added six that pp.167-170 cannot print -- Risk Management, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, Airport, Horizons, Water Resources. The six departments that are not division slugs are unchanged; adding divisions did not add any of them.

AND A CLAIM ABOUT THIS BEAD ELSEWHERE WAS FALSE AND IS CORRECTED. internal/check/fundingsources.go's doc said this decision "has to be made before fisc-7q6 maps the same fourteen pages at the division tier and carries a department on every row". fisc-7q6 has landed and needed nothing from it: its 292 facts each carry a DIVISION slug, which resolves fine, because the Expenditures by Category block is printed BY DIVISION. The two blocks on these pages sit on opposite sides of this bead's problem -- the upper one has a division to name, the lower one has only a department -- so that lane went round the decision rather than forcing it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR OPTION (a), which is the one that changes: the corpus now has a live example of both tiers on ONE PAGE, in two blocks whose totals are equal. If a fact may name either tier, p97 is where a reader meets both and where the projections would have to know which they are looking at. That is a better test case than anything available when this was filed.

Option (b) is unchanged and still a lie about the file's structure. Option (c) is partly done: internal/check/fundingsources.go and data/taxonomy.yaml both say so now.
close_reason:
DISCHARGED as option (a), across 8dfdb38 + 98fd6a4 + ba1b99f. A fact may now name either tier: check.Vocabulary gained Department(slug) bool, fact-departments-resolve resolves against division-OR-department, and the summary reports the two tiers separately so a schedule silently re-graining itself shows up as a count rather than passing unseen. Measured on the corpus now: '536 facts name one of 29 divisions and 264 facts name one of 6 departments'.

THIS BEAD'S OPTION LIST NEEDED A FOURTH ITEM THAT NOBODY HAD FOUND, and it is the reason (a) was not one commit. Two of the eleven department slugs -- community-development and public-works -- were ALSO data/taxonomy.yaml category slugs, and the registry refused that collision only for DIVISIONS. Measured: typing the department on pp.85-125's rows over the unrelaxed check gave 452 findings, of which 188 were this class and not the six-departments class this bead names. So (a) required the refusal to reach the department tier first, and required the two live collisions to be renamed public-works-function and community-development-function on library-function's precedent -- the suffix on the taxonomy side, because a department slug is a mechanical transform of a printed ALL-CAPS heading and departments.yaml derives nothing.

THE GUARD THIS BEAD SAID WAS THE POINT IS NOW PAID FOR, and it was measured rather than assumed. netCells refuses a fact carrying a department; these facts now carry one. Mutation: funding-city-council re-scoped to all-funds-gross now fails at projection build with 'sankey: fact fisc-f-f3444bece555 (livermore-budget-fy2026-2027 p85 "General Fund") carries department "city-council"' and drags five checks red. Before ba1b99f the same mutation built and exported clean and only funding-sources-tie-to-spine saw it.

OPTION (c)'s WRITTEN TRACES ARE CORRECTED IN THE SAME COMMITS: data/taxonomy.yaml's 'AND THE FACTS CARRY NO department: EITHER' and internal/check/fundingsources.go's 'AND THE SECOND GUARD DOES NOT REACH HERE EITHER' are both now false and both were rewritten. (c) still stands for acfr-general-fund-summary's five General Government rows, for a reason of that page's own -- two of them are department-level aggregates spanning several divisions -- and taxonomy.yaml now says that is a property of that page's grain rather than this bead's answer.

title: [bug] A row whose label is a bare fund name has its fund checked by nothing
description:
TWO CHECKS LOOK LIKE THEY COVER THIS AND NEITHER DOES.

row-funds-match-their-anchors (internal/check/rowfunds.go) reads a fund off the
row's own printed label, but only through rowAnchorPrefixes at :41-44 --
"Transfer From " (far) and "to ". resolveAnchorFund returns ok=false when no
prefix matches, on the stated ground that "no declared verb phrase, so the
anchor says nothing about direction and this check has no claim to make about
it". That reasoning is right about DIRECTION and wrong about IDENTITY: a row
labelled "Cal Home Reuse" names a fund unambiguously even though it names no
direction.

rule-funds-match-their-headings (internal/check/rulefunds.go) cannot cover it
either: declaredFund reads Parts[].Columns[].Fund only, so a rule that puts the
fund on the ROW declares zero funds and never enters the sweep.

WHAT IS EXPOSED. fisc-71j publishes 78 rows across pp.85-125 whose labels are
bare fund names and whose fund numbers are hand-typed. Five of those labels
match an operating fund AND its CIP twin in data/funds.yaml. Every CIP twin is
type: capital, so a wrong-twin fund moves money out of its group and WOULD be
